speakeroldname: Hon. Ron Basford (Minister of State for Urban Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister of State for Urban Affairs
subsubtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF PROGRAMS TO MAKE MORE SUBSIDIZED UNITS AVAILABLE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, for some time we have been seeking alternatives to the large public housing projects we have been building in conjunction with the provinces and at the same time seeking ways to make more units available to those on lower income who need them.
The new amendments to the National Housing Act presently before this House will offer more desirable alternatives to public housing, but I am pleased today to announce three new program proposals under the existing legislation, the National Housing Act, whereby more units of subsidized housing will be made available, and whereby a desirable social mix of low-income families and middle-income families can be obtained by using ordinary apartment and townhouse complexes.
First, in certain privately owned and financed buildings, a federal-provincial partnership will lease 25 per cent of the units for low-income people. The tenants will pay the same rate as in public housing with the two governments sharing the deficit on a 50-50 basis.
Concurrently, a second alternative program we are suggesting is to lease space in projects financed by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation under the limited dividend and non-profit sections of the housing act. In future, loans by CMHC in certain municipalities will be conditional upon 25 per cent of the units being made available to the federal-provincial partnership for low-income tenants.
At the same time, a third alternative program is being established to improve the social mix in subsidized housing by allowing non-subsidized middle-income people to live in publicly-owned housing on an experimental basis.
I am hopeful that our efforts to encourage a better mix of families by housing low-income people in privately-owned buildings will be welcomed by the private sector. I am pleased to announce that arrangements have been concluded with the province of Ontario to experiment with these changes. The Hon. Allan Grossman, the minister responsible for the Ontario Housing Corporation, and myself are making a statement in more detail on this today. An invitation to all provinces is being issued by me to take advantage of these new techniques for providing housing for those that need it most.

subsubtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF PROGRAMS TO MAKE MORE SUBSIDIZED UNITS AVAILABLE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to respond to the minister's statement I should like to say first of all that we are generally quite pleased that the government has taken this step. We think it is a constructive move and one that we hope will be expanded upon if it turns out to be a successful venture.
I should like to mention, however, that we hope that the minister, by making this statement or in his reference to legislation that will be coming before the House probably this week, is in no way failing to look at the true problem that exists at the present time in many of our urban areas, that is, the high cost of serviced land. We believe that is the root cause for much of the housing problems in this country and that his department should direct its attention to solving that basic problem as it has become almost critical, certainly in areas such as metropolitan Toronto.
Dealing generally with this statement, we welcome it.

speakerposition: N.D.P. Caucus Chair
subsubtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF PROGRAMS TO MAKE MORE SUBSIDIZED UNITS AVAILABLE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the members of the New Democratic Party welcome the statement made by the minister a few minutes ago. Like the minister, we believe there is a need to increase the mix of housing available to low-income Canadians. The proposals outlined in the minister's sketchy statement seem to move in a basically desirable direction. Having said that, I should like to raise three problems associated with the statement.
First, when the minister announced about a year ago his new scheme for assisted home ownership it was seen initially as the alternative, in the sense of replacement, for public housing in Canada. Very appropriately, there was almost wholesale rejection of that idea by those who have any degree of expertise and concern about housing for low income citizens. Since that time the minister, as I understand him, has either changed his position or corrected the impression that we are not to have a cutback in public housing as such but are going to add to it by broadening the range of choice. The crucial test, however, will be the amount of money provided by the government for low-income housing regardless of the type. That is the area we will be looking at with considerable interest. There is every justification for increasing the total amount of money spent on low-income housing in Canada, and as a party we certainly would not accept a policy that resulted in spending merely the same amount of money but shifting it from one category of low-income housing to another. We need a substantial increase in total outlay.
The second point I should like to make involves a matter of some concern. We must look at the details of implementation of the proposal to provide in privately owned and financed residences space for low-income people which in effect would be subsidized by Central

Mortgage and Housing Corporation or by the federal government. Our concern, if we are to move in the direction of providing accommodation for low-income people in privately financed buildings, is the degree of profit that will accrue to the people who own these private buildings. We do not want to see repeated any kind of financial rip-off on the part of developers on this area. What could happen is that they would take a certain limited percentage of low-income tenants but the level of financial support by the taxpayers of Canada could go well beyond the amount required merely to subsidize, if you like, in a socially necessary way the low-income people and simply provide very lucrative profit margins for private corporations.
The third point concerns the absence in this statement of any reference to moving in a significant way toward co-operative housing. The housing legislation that, hopefully, we will be discussing soon does contain some provisions in respect of co-op housing, but essentially as we read the legislation the provisions for co-operative housing projects to be supported in a significant financial way by the government are essentially of a charitable nature. We believe we must change and make owner-occupied co-op housing of the apartment type or single family separate unit type appealing to low-income Canadians. That is really what we see as a significant alternative to public housing of the kind we have had up to this point. This will require some changes in the bill that will come before us soon, and we will be pushing for them.
The final point I would like to make concerns land. There can be no doubt that the most significant aspect in housing today is the increasing cost of land for both public and private housing. The minister has made the right kind of signs that he is interested in dealing with that question, but we all know that nothing will be done about the matter of land unless the minister puts up millions of dollars for a significant land banking system. Therefore we support any move in this direction. But in the most serious way we enter the kind of caveats I have just mentioned in commenting on the minister's statement.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we welcome the announcement that the hon. minister has just made; however, we consider it to be but a very small step forward, since the minister did not mention the prices of land and utilities.
For each family to own its own home, I think one would have to see that utilities provided by municipalities were subsidized by the CMHC or by some other body, so that the cost of utilities would not have to be assumed by the owners of new houses. Utilities for a lot with 50 feet of frontage often cost as much as $40 or $45 a month for 20 years. If one adds to that the 11 per cent sales tax on building materials and the alarming rise of construction prices, which can be as high as $18,000 or $19,000 for a four-room one-family house, one can see that it is very difficult for small wage earners, getting between $4,000 and $5,000 a year, to buy a house. We do, however, note that the hon. minister intends the new legislation to benefit the category of those who earn from $4,000 to $5,000 a

year, who did not benefit under the former act, and to help them to become homeowners some day.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this bill is to amend the Canadian Citizenship Act to provide, in the case of a married woman who is a Canadian citizen residing outside of Canada, that her child born outside of Canada shall have the same right for her child to be a natural born Canadian citizen as the father and as an unmarried woman. subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-NEGLIGENCE OF GOVERNMENT RESPECTING UNEMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
That this House deplores the continuous increase in unemployment, as well as the refusal or negligence of the Government to propose effective measures for providing more jobs of a remunerative character for Canadians, and condemns the existing authorities for imposing and tolerating quasi-repressive measures affecting citizens who merely want to see respected their fundamental right to a decent standard of living and their personal dignity and to live in a climate of freedom and security.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I am proud to present this motion in the name of my colleagues of the Social Credit Party of Canada. Perhaps I will be criticized for harping on the same subject following the motions previously intro-

duced, but I wanted this motion to be more precise and concrete so as to enable us to put before the government true proposals which, if accepted, will eliminate the present climate of fear which is prevalent not only among the unemployed but even among those who now have a job and who do not know whether they will not be unemployed tomorrow.
For many years our unemployment rate has been steadily increasing. This unemployment rate is much too high for a still young nation, where much is left to be developed and which has still to meet the needs of one third of its population in the field of consumer goods.
In view of our high production capability and of the high demand for goods from handicapped and disadvantaged people living below the poverty line or even at the poverty line, I wonder about our hesitation to implement true solutions to this situation.
For the last few years we have been told that poverty was being fought; we have been hearing from time to time the leaders of our successive governments say that they were fighting unemployment. They mentioned "unemployment" but finally it turned out that it was a fight against the unemployed because the remedies proposed were probably the same as those which had been unefficient in the past.
So we need not be surprised that the employment situation in Canada is going from bad to worse. In fact, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) was saying as an excuse recently in a conference that if he had not succeeded in bringing down the unemployment rate, it was because too many new workers were coming on the labour market, too many young people offering to do some work to satisfy the requirements of the population, which in my view is a very poor excuse.
I think that the Prime Minister ought to have known last year, just as two or five years ago, that this situation would persist. Each year, a number of young people are coming on the labour market, and since it is impossible to satisfy them, a climate of fear has settled in this country, especially among the young people who are afraid that they will not be able to find a job upon completion of their studies.
Such fear also plagues adults, fear of losing one's job, or of being unable to find one, for lack of education.
There is also the fear of not being able to keep one's job because of automation, or of being displaced through automation and assigned to menial, less remunerated tasks.
The worker also fears inability to support his family, fears to start a family, with such a dismal outlook. It is a disturbing fear that healthy realism, a return to more rational notions of the purpose of the economy, and of work, could alleviate.
Mr. Speaker, what then is the purpose of economic activity and industrial work. Why do men gather in factories, in working communities, if not to achieve results unobtainable in isolation?
Now what results are sought after? The factory-owner might reply: profits. The worker's reply will be: earning a
March 12, 1973

living, drawing a salary. But neither profit nor salary matter, unless they bring about the satisfaction of needs.
But how are those needs met? They are met when the industrialist and the workers find goods capable of satisfying those needs. The purpose then of economic activity is not profit, nor salaries, but the production of goods and services that will satisfy human needs.
In his Reponse a des problemes d'aujourd'hui Jean Daujat explains simply: "The purpose of every economic activity, taken from the point of view of man's real wellbeing, can only be that of providing all the resources required by family life."
And so, the purpose of economic activity is the wellbeing of the family, the home, and therefore the consumer.
In his encyclical Quadragesimo Anno Pope Pius XI had already expressed in these terms the purpose of the economy, and I quote:
The economic and social structure will be soundly constituted only when it can give each and everyone of its members all the goods the resources of nature and industry, as well as the truly social organization of economic life can procure.
Mr. Speaker, so as to provide for those in need, for all families, for Canadian consumers, restricting laws such as we have today, the Unemployment Insurance Act for instance, must necessarily be replaced by a guaranteed annual income.
A British economist, now a consulting economist with the American government, Mr. Robert Theobald, has recommended some time ago the payment of a guaranteed annual income and a salary to students, at the 51st Annual Congress of the International Association of Personnel in Employment Security. This speech is summarized in the September 1964 issue of the Labour Gazette, a publication of the federal Department of Labour.
Mr. Speaker, the federal government has absolutely no excuse for being unaware of that suggestion since a publication of the federal Department of Labour has published it.
Mr. Theobald's theory is as follows, and I quote:
I believe we are entering a new era whose requirements are as different from those of the recent industrial age as those of the industrial age were different from those of the preceding agricultural age.
Today, the cybernated productive system is emerging-a new innovation in productive techniques and organization based on machine power and machine skill, i.e., on the combination of automated machinery and the computer. Two main aspects of the cybernation revolution are that it will force man's mind out of the productive system just as surely as the industrial revolution forced out man's muscle; and that the coming of cybernation means that there will be no effective limit to our productive abilities.
I believe that the effects of cybernation will in fact be so far-reaching and rapid that it will be impossible to achieve full employment: in other words, that the growing efficiency of machine systems will continue to increase so fast that employers- both government and private-will find it cheaper to own or hire machines rather than men.
Full employment can never be achieved, but even if it was, there are groups who should have a guaranteed income: those too old or too ill to hold a job; those with responsibilities that require that 25789-61J

they should not be under the obligation to hold a job, e.g., a woman with children but no husband, and those being educated.
May I quote further from the Labour Gazette:
To bring about his proposed guaranteed income, Mr. Theobald advocated a change in the United States Employment Act of 1946 that would make it the policy of the Government to provide job opportunities or to guarantee an income for anyone who was seeking work. He suggested that the starting level of the guaranteed income should be $1,000 for each adult and $600 for each child. In discussing the payment of students, Mr. Theobald said, "We must recognize that the student is already 'working' at least as relevantly as the man in the factory. The time has come when we must introduce the concept of a student salary, starting possibly at 14, and increasing with age, payable to all students attending school or university."
Mr. Speaker, that thesis was submitted to the American government seven or eight years ago. What was true then is all the more so today because, in Canada as elsewhere, especially in industralized countries, we have dug ourselves even deeper trying to achieve full employment, which is precisely where the government has erred.
Others have spoken along the same lines. I have here the opinion of an industrialist, and I quote:
John I. Snyder is president of United States Industries, comprising companies with a turnover of more than $114 million a year.
In an interview to Dun's Review, published by Dun and Brad-street Publications, for industrialists, businessmen and financiers, Snyder is explicit and goes straight to the point. He endorses Robert Theobald's proposals and believes that the separation of work and income concepts must be accepted, and measures taken to ensure to each person a guaranteed income, whether he is working or not.
Thirty-two economists are of the same opinion.
Thirty-two American economists, businessmen, union leaders have sent President Johnson, of the United States, a brief in which they ask the President of the U.S. to apply their suggestions, if the United States are to avoid "an economic and social chaos beyond description".
This was when Mr. Johnson was president of the United States. So, Americans are confronted with this economic chaos today, as much as Canadians are. Let me quote further:
As a first stage, it is essential to recognize that traditional relationships between employment and income are broken. An affluent economy can bring all citizens comfort and economic security, whether or not they are engaged in what is usually referred to as "work". We recommend therefore that society, through appropriate legal and government institutions, make the solemn commitment of providing every indidividual and family with an adequate income. The right to a guaranteed income for all will replace the patchwork of present social measures which range from unemployment to direct assistance.
This is a very specific proposition.
Now, here are a few opinions from labour leaders.
In "Positions syndicales face a l'automatisation", George Levard, the Secretary General of the Confederation frangaise des Travailleurs Chretiens, says, and I quote:
"If we are to avoid congestion, automated industry will have to come to "secrete" purchasing power as well as its products. But it will not be possible, for the most part, to bestow this purchasing power on people proportionally to the role they have played in production. It will have to be a SOCIAL, or SOCIALIZED, purchasing power, by which I mean one that aims at promoting mass consumption".

March 12, 1973
Unemployment
And now we hear Canadian unions saying the same thing. For example, at the biennial CLC Congress that took place in Montreal from April 20 to 24, 1964, the CLC vice-president, Mr. William Dodge, told 2,000 delegates, and I quote:
"Let us suppose that in spite of work development programs and the best of training courses and placement systems, technological changes resulted in a continuous decrease in the demand for manpower. What would happen if technological changes threatened to destroy the labour market itself? We would then have to revise our codes of ethnics and state that everyone has a right to be fed, clothed, educated and cared for even if he produces nothing".
William Dodge foresaw in 1964 that the regional economic development measures aimed at job planning in Canada, adult training courses and other measures the government suggested, would all come to nothing. Indeed, it has left very little hope to Canadian workers.
So, Mr. Speaker, that is why the Liberal government has failed in its fight against unemployment. It wanted to attain full employment which has now been found to be impossible. So much time lost. So many sufferings needlessly experienced by rejected workers who are even blamed for promises made to them.
Why go on in that direction? Why persist in resorting to a remedy which is doomed to fail? Why not try instead to establish a guaranteed minimum income plan which would enable the entire population to take advantage of already available goods which the able-bodied workers are eager to produce? Why not get off the beaten track? Is the government afraid of making innovations, of satisfying the Canadian people? What is preventing it from acting?
It would be interesting, Mr. Speaker, to hear the answer this evening when the minister answering on behalf of the government will be in the House. I regret he is not here this afternoon. He has been delayed because of bad weather. He has not been as foreseeing as I. I got up at two o'clock this morning, I took my car and left for Ottawa. At any rate, I am told that the hon. minister will be there tonight, and I shall be pleased to hear the proposals he will put forward in an attempt to meet urgent requirements of Canadians.
We hear increasingly more about the guaranteed minimum income. Some people call it "a fair distribution of resources." This is how it is defined by the Canadian Welfare Council in an article published in Le Droit on January 29, 1969:
A program designed to secure a satisfactory guaranteed annual income, which the Canadian Welfare Council considers as a social right for all Canadians, should be introduced "as soon as possible".
If the just society is to be something more than a vain and fragile abstraction, it must be founded on some basic and intangible rights, including social rights, as well as civil and political ones. Among social rights, none is more important than the right to an adequate income. We must include right now this social economic objective in our system of values. The method to administer guaranteed income can be decided upon later on. If necessary, it can be introduced by stages.

Then, Mr. Speaker, this is another voice demanding that a guaranteed minimum income be established for everybody, to replace the annoying system we have at present.
In the motion I put forward, I speak of citizens who require that their basic right be respected in order to reach an adequate standard of living. Now, it is noticed that certain public servants almost compell them to beg to have their vested rights respected. As for unemployment insurance, I have some very eloquent testimonies which show that this legislation is far from being efficient and falls short of meeting the needs of Canadians.
It is undoubtedly because this is a bureaucratic law giving rise to a dreadful amount of red tape that government employees themselves find most difficult to handle.
At LaSarre, where I live, there is an unemployment insurance sub-office to answer the needs of the population. During the week, when I am in Ottawa, my wife receives each day scores of telephone calls from people asking for my help in having their rights respected in the field of unemployment insurance benefits. I want to record in Hansard a few very special and specific cases. I could talk until six o'clock, and possibly until eight to wait for the minister, but I will only quote a few examples.
Mr. Speaker, a lady from Saint-Gerard-de-Berry had difficulty in getting the unemployment insurance benefits that she was entitled to.
So I went into action when she told me about it and I received from the unemployment insurance service in Rouyn a copy of the following reply addressed to that lady on February, 13, 1973.1 quote:
On October 19, 1972, you requested that your file be transferred to this office. You wrote to tell us that you had received no employment insurance benefit, since your transfer request. We got in touch with our main office which, on February 6,1973 .. .
Note the interval between October 19, 1972 and February 6, 1973.
... sent you four money-orders as payment for the weeks from October 1,1972 to November 18, 1972.
In the case of that claimant, there was a 14-week delay before she could get the benefits she was entitled to, on account of a file transfer from one unemployment insurance office to another. For that reason and of that reason alone, the Unemployment Insurance Commission officials were almost unable to do anything. They are at a loss. It is the same thing every time a file is transferred. A letter was addressed to me by the former minister responsible for the Unemployment Insurance Commission, the hon. member for Verdun (Mr. Mackasey), and I quote:
Dear Mr. Laprise:
This is with reference to the June 5, 1972 letter from my special assistant concerning the unemployment insurance problem of Mr. Georges Audet, Val St-Gilles, Abitibi-Ouest, Quebec.
Revision of payments made to that recipient shows that it is the new procedure for issuing cheques which delayed payments for the period from March 19 to May 27,1972.
While the cheque issuing procedure was being changed, the unemployed had to tighten their belt, run into debt with the stores in order to survive, pending the change within the Unemployment Insurance Commission.

I shall now cite a case involving another beneficiary. I myself contacted the Unemployment Insurance Office in Rouyn, and they informed me that his claim was valid from March 22, 1972, and that he received payments for 25 consecutive weeks. The problem of the beneficiary Mr. Alfred St-Pierre, of La Sarre, is that, after 25 weeks of unemployment, he found a job for himself. It was a temporary job.
Unfortunately, that job lasted too long: he worked for five weeks. When there was no more work, he wanted to receive unemployment insurance payments again, but because he had worked longer than four weeks-he had worked five-he had lost his right to claim. If he had not worked, he could have claimed for another 26 weeks, but because he had worked for five weeks, he lost everything; as the regulation eight weeks were not up, giving him the right to apply again, he lost all claim to unemployment insurance.
Mr. Speaker, when we find laws like this still in existence, we wonder where the government's advisers were and what they had in mind when the bill covering unemployment insurance was "patented". Unemployment Insurance Commission investigators travel the regions of Hamilton, Toronto, Montreal, Hull, etc., in search of beneficiaries who do not want to work. When they come across cases like the one I have just described, I should think they have their work cut out to get him back on their lists.
I have before me another case where the benefits were delayed for 20 weeks before the unemployed's rights were met.
In another case, an individual was entitled to 15 weeks of unemployment insurance benefits on account of illness, but due to an error of the Unemployment Insurance Commission, he got his benefits only five months later.
I shall mention another case involving not the local unemployment office of my area, but that of the Terrebonne area, and more precisely that of Saint-Jerome; again, a citizen had his unemployment insurance benefits delayed by five months. There are dozens of such cases.

If such is not the case, I am going to read the motion again for the benefit of the two hon. members who spoke.
The motion reads as follows:
That this House deplores the continuous increase in unemployment, as well as the refusal or negligence of the Government to propose effective measures for providing more jobs of a remunerative character for Canadians, and condemns the existing authorities of imposing or tolerating quasi-repressive measures affecting citizens who merely want to see respected their fundamental right to a decent standard of living and their personal dignity and to live in a climate of freedom and security.
Mr. Speaker, I think I have just shown quite clearly that there are measures which are not only quasi-repressive but repressive for many unemployment insurance claimants, whether they be claiming standard unemployment insurance benefits or claiming unemployment benefits for reasons of illness.
I have just submitted several cases of hardship wheree claimants were denied benefits for many weeks. If this is not enough, I can go back to my office and come back with many more. If those hon. members who raised the

March 12, 1973
Unemployment
issue are interested, I think that my colleagues will be able to quote several cases in the course of the day.
Mr. Speaker, as I said earlier, it is not only a matter of criticizing the present situation, there must be solutions proposed. In order to avoid all the problems caused by social legislation taken here and there, we are calling for a guaranteed minimum income system which would affect everybody, regardless of their social situation and their age.
Instead of telling the Canadian consumer to be satisfied with the little he gets, to tighten his belt and to make do with $28 a week, this government should see to it that all Canadians have the necessary purchasing power to meet Canadian production, which would have the effect of stimulating demand, encouraging agricultural production and ensuring at the same time supplementary income for Canadian farmers.
During the last election campaign, Mr. Speaker, we offered the Canadian electorate a guaranteed minimum income plan which would have precisely given satisfaction to everybody and which would not have cost more than all the systems we have now.
When we make propositions, Mr. Speaker, we get the answer: Where are we going to take the money? Those same people never ask themselves: Where are we going to take the money to pay the interest on the public debt to big financiers. This year it stands at $2.5 billion.
When it is a matter of relieving misery, of reassuring those who are afraid of what is in store for them, those who fear unemployment and loss of income, they shout: Where shall we get the money? When it is a matter of meeting the requirements of high finance, the government is all eyes and ears and ready to give everything to satisfy them.
Mr. Speaker, even if the minister has not heard what I have just said, I hope his colleagues will inform him of the motion I have introduced so that he be able to give to the two thirds of Canadians who live in anxiety and misery at least a glimpse of hope by telling them that in a few weeks legislation will solve their problems and help them live well and draw from the abundant riches Canada possesses.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-NEGLIGENCE OF GOVERNMENT RESPECTING UNEMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
I did not
object in order to attribute any particular fault to the hon. member, or to take exception to what he had been saying in his interesting speech. But when the government whip interjected I became confused because I was under the impression Mr. Speaker had indicated that the hon. member's time had expired. At the same time, I saw him attempting to pursue his deliberations. I am sorry the deputy leader of the Social Credit party was so sensitive in those circumstances.
The motion as presented contains, it appears to me, three main propositions. First, it deplores the continuous increase in unemployment. This, of course, is what we on this side have been doing for the past four and a half years. It seems to me we have suffered an inexcusable level of unemployment, one which ought not to be tolerated in a country such as Canada. For years we have been protesting against the attitude of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) in adopting fiscal and monetary policies which largely brought about the present unemployment situation. I cannot find words adequate to express the suffering which has resulted from this philosophy. I will admit that the government appears at this time to have learned its lesson. On the other hand, it has brought down a budget which many of us on this side feel is inadequate in the circumstances, and that to this extent the government has not learned its lesson.
The second point on which the motion places emphasis is the government's refusal to propose effective measures to provide more jobs of a remunerative character for Canadians. This is another aspect which we on this side have continuously stressed and it is one which must be brought home. Obviously, with the annual growth in the size of the labour force, we must take steps to stay ahead. The government has not yet come to grips with this situation. In the United States, at the last count, unemployment had declined to some 5 per cent. In Canada, on the other hand, the rate is something over 6 per cent, leaving us with some 600,000 people unemployed. Germany is all right. Japan is all right. I cannot understand why this question of unemployment was not given priority, and
March 12, 1973

why more effort was not made to create jobs to take up the slack. We know the labour force has increased in numbers. In consequence, our goal should be to develop national economic growth to ensure unemployment will steadily decline. I shall deal with this aspect later in connection with what spokesmen for this party had to say about the budget.
The motion makes a third point-the problem which has arisen in connection with unemployment insurance. There has been talk about gestapo tachcs and police state methods. Mr. Speaker, the vast majority of people ih Canada do not want cheaters to take advantage of unemployment insurance. They want them to be ferreted out and removed from the safe haven they occupy at the expense of the taxpayers' pocket. After all, it is the taxpayers, including the man who is working day in and day out, whether for a low income or a high income, who are bearing the cost of this haven, and they are becoming very concerned about it as well as the situation in which the Unemployment Insurance Commission finds itself. We on this side believe there ought to be some method by which the cheats and abusers are ferreted out. Until such time as this is accepted as part of the Commission's function, a great deal of disillusionment is bound to arise among those who are paying the shot. At the same time, care should be taken to avoid ill-considered actions.
I have here a couple of press cuttings, one of them from the Evening Patriot which circulates in the Kitchener-Waterloo area. The headline over a leading article reads: "Let's be really sure the innocent don't suffer". I think we are all concerned about this aspect. That is why I am pleased the minister has indicated that the advisory committee on the UIC is looking into the investigatory procedures of the benefit control officers to determine whether they are approaching this work with a measure of compassionate understanding. The article reads:
Undoubtedly many persons have cheated on the Unemployment Insurance Act. The average citizen who prefers to do things in an honest manner has surely become annoyed over these thefts and applauds those who have been trying to remedy this situation.
I certainly agree with that. The article goes on:
However, in the attempt to rectify the affair there is always the danger that some innocent persons who deserve the benefits will suffer.
Here is another article, this one from the Toronto Star of March 6. I think the Star put its finger right on the problem, here. The headline over the editorial section reads: "Cheaters endanger unemployment pay". The article reads:
The whole system will be in jeopardy unless the public can be assured that deliberate idlers and cheats are going to be cut off. For the great majority of Canadians in the labour force still must work regularly for their living, whether they like it or not, and they cannot be expected to go on supporting freeloaders with their taxes.

speechtext: Would the hon. member permit a question?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-NEGLIGENCE OF GOVERNMENT RESPECTING UNEMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Certainly.
Unemployment

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-NEGLIGENCE OF GOVERNMENT RESPECTING UNEMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
The hon. member has just said that the unemployment rate is only 5 per cent in the United States, Mr. Speaker.
Does the hon. member take into account the fact that the United States were exporting a great part of their unemployment to Canada because of the draft dodgers who came to settle here because the United States were at war until recently?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-NEGLIGENCE OF GOVERNMENT RESPECTING UNEMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Well, I do not intend to be distracted in that direction. Notwithstanding the situation there, the United States seems to have realized that high unemployment cannot be tolerated in a society such as theirs. They have used all their expertise and all their wisdom to see that opportunities for work are available, and thus they have been able to reduce the unemployment level to 5 per cent. All I want to say is that we in Canada should show the same foresight and understanding so as to create a climate in the economy generally which will ensure that those who want to work will have the opportunity. Certain members opposite have cast doubt upon the validity of the work ethic. This is not a philosophy which this young country needs. The work ethic built this country. The work ethic is building it now. The appreciation of the work ethic will continue to build this country and lead us to our ultimate destiny, one of the leading industrial nations of the world. With regard to unemployment insurance, the article in the Star then reads:
To save the system, then, the government must sternly detect and disqualify people who abuse unemployment insurance-even if this crackdown displeases the Liberals' temporary allies, the New Democrats.
I do not mention that to be partisan. I just want to let members know that the vast majority of Canadians are sick and tired of having the unemployment insurance fund abused. It is our function to try to devise with compassion a scheme whereby the innocent will not suffer. If members opposite want to get involved in this debate, all they have to do is go to their whip, put their names on the list and, if they have been good boys, they will have that opportunity.
I wish to return to my first point about unemployment. Bill C-124, the bill that removed the ceiling on the Unemployment Insurance Fund, was introduced and, because of the fact we were not able to get any forecasts with respect to what would be considered an unacceptable level of unemployment in the future, I respectfully suggest that we are in trouble again, no matter what the minister says about his budget.
As we pointed out, the budget is not expansionary enough. When Bill C-124 repealed the $800 million limit on the contribution that could be made to the fund, the Canadian people were left in the dark. Even if we talk about unemployment insurance, we have to be concerned because this government still does not realize that the way to cut the cost of unemployment is to increase the number of employed Canadians. That is the answer to this problem, not to create a bureaucratic nightmare. We must admit that a whole employment policy is desperately required and to this end all our attention should be direct-

March 12, 1973
Unemp loyment
ed. The cold, hard figures show that this government has plagued Canada with high unemployment for the past four and one half years. There were 688,000 Canadians out of work in January, the largest number recorded for the month in a decade. We cannot pooh-pooh that.

speechtext: You said that.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-NEGLIGENCE OF GOVERNMENT RESPECTING UNEMPLOYMENT
speechtext: I said it and I will continue repeating it. The hon. member must learn that we cannot accept 688,000 Canadians out of work. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) said that we cannot continually talk about numbers and statistics. He was right.

speechtext: Can I ask a question?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-NEGLIGENCE OF GOVERNMENT RESPECTING UNEMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
No, you cannot. After all, we only have 20 minutes. You can make your speech and then we will understand what you are trying to say.
We must not forget the cost of unemployment. We are talking about billions of dollars. What figure can be put on the frustration of those who generally work and support their families but cannot, so have had their family life soured by unemployment? Real people are behind these figures, heads of families, some 180,000 men, women who must supplement their husband's incomes and our young people. Those between the ages of 15 and 25 make up a huge percentage of the unemployed. What are we doing for them? Are we giving them any hope for the future? The hon. member laughs. This is a very ticklish situation. I have watched the climate that has been created amongst our youth. They are not too happy with what is happening. The hon. member ought to know that. They are looking for opportunities and there are no opportunities. They want to work, but there is no work. We can sit back and play hide-and-seek with them. We can take a complacent attitude. We can appear as though we do not have any concern. This is what they think. This is all I am saying.
We must attempt to talk about economic growth and industrial strategy. You can use all those phrases. Once you acquire full employment, whether we are down to 4.5 per cent unemployment or not-whatever we may call that-we are then able to acquire the tax dollars which will allow us to give our senior citizens more money, reduce the eligible age for old age security to 60 and allow us the wherewithal for all the social programs that are required in this very frustrating life today. This is what we are talking about. Conditions should be created so that those who want to work can work. Lord knows, everybody wants to work. If the opportunity is not there, we are the losers. The Canadian taxpayer is the loser because he is paying twice. He is not only paying his income taxes but he is paying for an unemployment insurance scheme of which the vast majority of Canadians will never take advantage. That is why he is concerned.
Members opposite know what our party has indicated. If members opposite want me to read the list, I will do so. If we had been in office, we would have brought before parliament a budget which would have provided substantial stimulation to the economy and would have provided for a 90 day freeze on prices and incomes. Fresh food would be exempt from the freeze. Our program for cutting unemployment, in addition to the tax cuts and pension increases proposed by the Minister of Finance, would

consist of eliminating the sales tax on building materials. How long have we been calling for that? I bet the Liberals will eventually steal that one, too. Eliminating the 11 per cent sales tax on building materials would enhance construction, give some impetus to construction, provide houses and employment. We would have removed the sales tax on all clothing rather than merely for children up to 14 years of age which will create a bureaucratic nightmare determining who is up to what age and what size.
We would have introduced an incentive program to encourage investment in small Canadian business. We have said on several occasions that $2,500 invested by a Canadian should give him a tax credit. It is in this area of manufacturers that we have to look for leadership with respect to employment. These are the people who need that incentive. As I understand it, the vast majority of employment comes from the little fellow who employs three, four or five people. We are the ones who say "buy Canadian" and encourage nationalistic instincts. Let us do something to encourage Canadians to invest. This is a point we would have introduced.
The 90 day freeze on prices and incomes would be used to consult with the provinces, businessmen, union leaders and consumer groups about the range of guidelines we would use after the freeze. The freeze would be part of a long-term plan to both cut unemployment and contain inflation. We in this party believe the Canadian people would accept the freeze because it would be part of a double- pronged assault on unemployment and inflation. The public has lost faith in a succession of Liberal finance ministers. They have no faith in their attempts to solve this problem. We came out with a bold and imaginative step, freezing wages and price controls. The government has discussed this. I hear they had a whale of a debate in their caucus. They did not even think we would submit that idea.
I notice there has been general acceptance of this twopronged attack, a completely expansionary budget with a freeze in order that we could meet with labour and management to determine where we are going. Hon. members opposite do not think that we would do this, but they realize now it is not a bad idea. Yesterday we were told that inflation has gone up 5.8 per cent and it is now the highest it has been for 22 years. When we ask the government what their contingency plans are, the reply is that they have something around the corner. It takes courage and guts to do what we suggest, but with an expansionary budget one must be concerned about inflation. This is why we propose a two-pronged attack.
I am a little concerned about what is happening with the UIC. For some reason or other the government brought in Bill C-125 which, let us say, places a more than usual onus on the employee. The House reconvened on January 4, yet the government has not introduced a modified bill that would define such things as "being fired for misconduct", "availability for employment", "just cause" and "without good cause". These are burning questions that must be answered.
March 12, 1973

This bill was supposed to save the Canadian taxpayers $100 million. We are now into the middle of March and no bill has been introduced that would-

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-NEGLIGENCE OF GOVERNMENT RESPECTING UNEMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it saddens me somewhat to follow the previous speaker because, although he sounds so compassionate and sincere in his delivery, he reminds me of those right wingers in 1937, 1938 and 1939 when I was unemployed, a time when the premier of the province of British Columbia told us to root, hog or die. At that time the mayor of the city of Vancouver read the riot act and set the police on us because we were "lazy, no good bums". While the hon. member does not use those words, he is using a similar line of argument.
What bothers me about what the previous speaker said is that he professes to be speaking on behalf of the workers of Canada who object to having their money used to pay for those lazy, no good bums who are drawing unemployment insurance. Personally, I would rather see 2 per cent of the people who are unemployed cheating the Unemployment Insurance Act than adopt some of the recommendations made by members to my right to cut people off unemployment insurance. Less than 2 per cent of the workers who are drawing unemployment insurance cheat. I suggest to the hon. member that he take a look at other professions in the country and sees who cheats on income tax and just about everything else, such as lawyers, doctors and some of the most respected people in this country. The figure is higher than 2 per cent once you start to check into it.
The type of expression that has emanated from the party to my right must be looked at very seriously. The hon. member talks about a freeze, and I now notice a change in wording. No longer is it a wage and prices freeze; it is a prices and incomes freeze, if you please. But regardless of the expression hon. members use, it is still a freeze, and there is no possible way that a freeze can be fair to the working people. This has been proven in England and in the United States where they implemented a wage freeze. The only thing that works is the freeze itself, since the employers control the wages. But you cannot control prices. In the United States inflation is skyrocketing, even with wage and price controls.
Instead of sitting down with labour leaders and having discussions, let us sit down with the money lenders of this country, or the owners of apartment complexes and houses who are ripping-off the working people by charging high rents. Let us talk about true incomes, not the incomes of working people. Their incomes are already controlled. Members of unions-one-third of the workers of Canada-already have their wages controlled. They have to negotiate, under laws that are written by provincial and federal governments, for periods of three months, four months, six months and up to a year before they get a wage increase. The wages of the other two-thirds of the workers not members of unions are really controlled. They are subject to the whims of their employers, who pay them what they want to pay. So, I suggest to hon. members that when they start talking about a freeze, they
Unemployment
should put a freeze on the money made by the rip-off artists in this country, not on the wages of the working people.
I have read the motion a number of times, but the only conclusion I can come to is that it is a motherhood motion. I do not see how anyone in their right mind could oppose it. Although the motion before us does not explicitly say so, I presume the latter part of it which deals with repressive measures, and so on, is some implied criticism of the present unemployment insurance administration, the act, and the tactics of the UIC benefit control officers. This is a matter to which I should like to refer.
I have represented the working people of Canada for 22 years and I know some of their problems. I have sat on boards of referees in the city of Vancouver for 12 years and I am aware of some of the problems created by the present act which confront the workers. It is very difficult to get on unemployment insurance rolls, and at times it is damned difficult to stay on them as a result of the attitude of those who administer the Unemployment Insurance Act. I speak for the working people, Mr. Speaker, and I truly believe that.
These people are the working men and women of Canada. In the main they comprise 85 per cent of the purchasing power of this country and account for nearly the same percentage of votes. They consider the present act to be a humane one and, quite frankly, one of the best unemployment insurance acts in the world. But they feel it needs some amendment, as do the regulations and some of the interpretations that have been placed on the act and the regulations by insurance officers, especially, I repeat, benefit control officers. It is my considered opinion that the basic criteria originally established for the Canadian unemployment insurance system in 1943 to provide a decent standard of living for the legitimately unemployed of this nation are being continuously eroded and undermined. Claimants today are finding the new Unemployment Insurance Act and regulations much more restrictive in their attempt to qualify for benefits and the retention of eligibility.
In light of this noticeable trend, I should like to make a few suggestions and recommendations. I want to deal first with benefit control officers. Many workers have already expressed their dissatisfaction with the interrogation that is conducted by officers under the provisions of section 107 of the act, and have made specific recommendations based on day to day experience as agents, officers, and members of boards of referees. They are familiar with the enunciated administrative policy of the Unemployment Insurance Commission in this matter, but I reiterate that the following amendments to this section would vastly improve the multitude of situations arising from the present interviewing process conducted by benefit control officers.
First one, by statute, a claimant should have the right at all times to a representative of his or her choice to be in attendance when interviews by benefit control officers are being conducted. Second, a claimant should be notified that he is not required to sign prepared statements, that such signatures to statements are purely voluntary,
2120

March 12, 1973
Unemployment
and should be signed only after complete agreement has been reached between the claimant and the interviewing officer as to the statements contained therein. Third, the claimant should be permitted to return signed statements, rather than having to sign them in the presence of the interviewing officer. Fourth, the claimant should be entitled to amend or reword the prepared statements to ensure that any signed statement clearly and specifically reflects his or her circumstances.
I should like to touch now on appeals to boards of referees and umpires. I have noted that the present Unemployment Insurance Commission forms notify the claimant of the right to appeal within 30 days of being disqualified or disentitled. I believe that such notice should be either in larger type or in a different colour to ensure the claimant's notice of the same. It is my opinion that many additional claimants would more readily utilize the board of referees if a statement on the notice of rejection by the Unemployment Insurance Commission to the claimant briefly explained the right of the claimant, the structure and jurisdiction of the board and, further, the general procedure the claimant is required to follow if he desires to initiate an appeal action to the umpire, if this becomes necessary. The insurance officers responsible for adjudication of claimants' cases should be thoroughly conversant with the appeal procedure. In my opinion, the claimant should be given this kind of additional information at this stage of processing to ensure that fairness and justice shall prevail for all.
In respect of notices of rejection, disqualification and disentitlement, I have noted that in many cases the Unemployment Insurance Commission did not include the specific and applicable section of the act or the regulations, and where this information was included to the claimant it did not clearly specify the specific reason or explanation of the provision in layman's language. I recommend that in cases of this nature, the unemployment insurance officers should be instructed to be more specific in the phraseology and terminology used to ensure that the specific reason in the individual claimant's case is not only clarified but readily understandable to the average claimant.
I should like to refer briefly to problems arising in respect of sections covering vacation and holiday payments. A multitude of problems have emanated directly from the present provisions contained under the regulatory parts of Sections 172 and 173. Let me enunciate them as follows: The adverse effects on claimants who are in receipt of earned vacation pay several months prior to the actual date mutually agreed upon as the vacation period by the claimant or his representative, through his union agreement; the detrimental effect to the claimant when such moneys are received within the period stipulated under Section 173(15), that is the six weeks' provision; in logging and construction industries, where employees work for numerous employers during the year and 6 per cent of gross earnings are automatically included by contractual provision, the sections have an unfair effect; the subsidizing effect to the Unemployment Insurance Commission fund of claimants who accept earned vacation pay at the time of layoff or separation and who, by mutual agreement, have already fixed a time period some six

weeks to two months in the future when they shall be returning to the same employer.
In my opinion, all moneys earned during a period preceding the date of separation from employment rightfully belong to the employee, regardless of when they are received. Such moneys should in no way be manipulated by any legislation which would result in the claimant being compelled to lose or be forced to reduce his or her purchasing power and right to earned vacation. This, in effect, results in direct subsidization by the claimant of the unemployment insurance fund and in many cases disqualifies and disentitles claimants from maximum coverage. I would therefore recommend that all moneys obtained in the form of vacation or holiday pay, etc., should in no way be used to prevent claimants from entitlement to unemployment insurance benefits in contrast to a claimant receiving no such remuneration.
Let me now refer to separation certificates. Many claimants undergo a great deal of personal frustration and delay in claim processing because of the lack of the employer's fulfillment of obligatory requirements as contained in Section 111 of the act, which reads:
Upon separation of an insured person from employment, the contributions payable for the current pay period and all other contributions then unpaid shall be paid by the employer immediately.
The terminology is clear and specific. Direction by the unemployment insurance office and others to claimants that it is the claimant's responsibility to provide an up-to-date separation certificate on separation, and to personally follow up any delay by his employer, is improper in my opinion. Employers should fulfil their obligations to the claimant, and where they do not I would urge that the Unemployment Insurance Commission or one of its officers take immediate remedial action on behalf of the affected claimant to prevent undue delays, time, effort and costs to all parties concerned.
I should like now to refer to the employer appeal section which has recently been put into the Unemployment Insurance Act. The employer's right to appeal has had disastrous results. A fine example is the action taken by employers in the forest products industry in British Columbia in the spring and summer of last year. In the fallers' dispute, one claimant appeal at the board of referees' level resulted in the rejection of approximately 4,000 claims already accepted and processed by the Unemployment Insurance Commission, Pacific region. This could have resulted in a possible 16,000 separate appeals before the board. Complications in that industry continued when approximately 5,000 additional claimants' rights to unemployment insurance were eventually challenged by the Unemployment Insurance Commission, Pacific region, and the specific large employers. This could have initiated an additional 25,000 separate appeals by those members. Fortunately for all concerned, sanity prevailed and an acceptable agreement for entitlements was eventually reached.
This and similar experiences have convinced me that this section has been and will continue to be abused by the employer, particularly during periods leading to major negotiation. I can readily understand the concern of some employers relative to the merit rating system. In fact, in
March 12, 1973

the aforementioned cases, the unions' representatives assisted the employers, satisfactorily resolving this major problem. I would recommend that the provisions in this matter be similar in principle to those contained in previous legislation, and that the present act be amended to provide for the deletion of the words "or an employer" in the first line of Section 94(1).
Referring now to the general resumption of work provision as interpreted under this present act, the criteria of 85 per cent is antiquated and, in most cases, serves no useful purpose. Discontinuation of production immediately after a labour dispute has been shown to be directly attributable to other causes, such as mutually agreed upon vacation periods, maintenance and overhaul requirements, climatic conditions, employees on sickness and compensation and other legitimate leaves of absence. For this reason, serious consideration must be given to a logical and sensible basis of determining what constitutes general resumption of work. This present 85 per cent provision should be abolished and criteria substituted which would be based on individual plant or industry circumstances obtaining immediately after a labour dispute.
With regard to Regulation 148(1) covering interruption of earnings and waiting periods, it is my belief that the waiting period presently required constitutes an unwarranted penalty against the claimant who, through no fault of his own, has become unemployed. The seven consecutive day provision discourages those claimants who could work a day or two a week after termination, but are hesitant to do so because such action would nullify establishment of the waiting period. I would recommend that the waiting period as such be revised to provide for any seven days in a consecutive 52-week period.
There is another section which really disturbs me having to do with the 25-day period. It is my understanding that in certain exempted industries, for example lumbering, landscaping, agriculture, etc., there is provision that employers and employees do not have to make UIC or CPP contributions if the employee works less that a 25-day period for any such employer. This situation has resulted in abuse by employers, resulting in no credits applicable or available from the aforementioned funds when required. I believe this section to be discriminatory in its intent and application and therefore request that credits be recognized for those employees in exempted industries for each and every day of employment.
I should like to deal now, if I may, with sick benefits and maternity coverage. Major attachment claimants who have established eligibility in the initial benefit period and who have received any payments of one dollar or more in the form of benefits are disqualified from payment of unemployment insurance benefits if they become ill or incapacitated in a subsequent extended benefit period. This new legislation is a contradiction of the principle applicable in Canada from'the inception of the unemployment insurance scheme and in force up to June 27, 1972, whereby eligible claimants on established claim received unemployment insurance payments for subsequent illnesses, injuries or incapacities as normally entitled claimants. I would urge, Mr. Speaker, that the restrictive provi-
Unemployment
sions presently contained be deleted and the previous principle and criteria be reintroduced for coverage purposes under similar circumstances.
I want to deal briefly with disentitlement by age or pension. Many employees are ready, available and capable of performing satisfactorily in various types of employment where they are compelled to retire due to employer policy or other reasons. Many such employees have, in most cases, contributed to the UIC for decades without any previous need for claim. The provisions of present section Section 31(1) (a) (b) and the special severance benefit provision I believe are restrictive and discriminatory. I believe an injustice is done to those claimants who are required under the present provisions of the act and regulations to be compelled by law to reimburse the Unemployment Insurance Commission more monies than they have actually been in direct receipt of, in cases where overpayments become applicable.
The requirement for the Unemployment Insurance Commission to deduct income tax on behalf of the taxation department for the claimant causes additional financial burden and hardship when claimants need to find additional moneys during unemployed periods. They have to reimburse the amount received by cheque from the Unemployment Insurance Commission and a further additional amount equal to the total income tax deductions forwarded by the Unemployment Insurance Commission on behalf of the claimant. In my opinion the claimant under those circumstances should be compelled to pay only the actual amount received on Unemployment Insurance Commission cheque forms.
I want to deal now with advisory committees, section 108. The establishment and retention of a regional advisory committee for unemployment insurance purposes is a subject which I believe warrants attention at this time. In my opinion, there has been a lack of communication by employers and employee representatives in an area or regional basis for the last ten years or so. An effective vehicle is required to keep the National Advisory Committee informed on an up-to-date basis as to problems and recommendations for solution and improvement.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as a member of the government party I welcome this particular motion because I think this is a subject, of which the government must be aware, although I do not for a moment accept the suggestion that it needs reminding of it. I believe that, from time to time, the opposition parties are not aware of many of the things the government is doing to assist the unemployed to obtain employment or to be taken care of when they are among the ranks of the unemployed. We have appreciated this obligation. As I have said, I believe it is the responsibility of the opposition parties to impress on the government that it has a responsibility in this area. However, by the same token I believe opposition parties have an obligation to tell us what they would do were they, heaven forbid, the government. When I listened to the hon. member for Abitibi (Mr. Laprise) present his views I thought we were here to talk
25789-62}

March 12, 1973
Unemployment
about the Unemployment Insurance Commission because he did not seem to get down to the crux of his motion.
I think an opposition day motion should properly be wide in scope, but I would have thought the hon. member would have dealt more with the unemployment issue and less with the Unemployment Insurance Commission. I could read a series of letters from constituents of mine, as the hon. member did, who from time to time have been displeased, upset or angry with the administration of this particular plan. As a former member of the committee on Labour, Manpower and Immigration, I might say that during the so-called recess in the month of September when other members were back in their constituencies doing a little politicking some of us came back to attend the Committee on Labour, Manpower and Immigration to put together this particular bill and give it clause by clause study. I believe this was a very good committee which operated in a co-operative manner. From time to time a little partisanship crept in, which is only natural, but I believe by and large the members of the committee were convinced this was, in fact, a good bill.
It disturbs me somewhat now to hear members of the official opposition knocking this particular measure, decrying the fact that they did not have more time or wishing that they had more information. But this is after the fact. This was not the position they took when the bill was being considered by the committee. I think when this bill came out of the committee we were all satisfied that we, in fact, had a good bill. When concern was expressed about the amount of money being put into the unemployment insurance fund by all the new people who had been brought into the plan and the increased benefits, there seemed to be a backing off from this bill by the official opposition. To their credit, the members of the New Democratic Party supported the bill which they had supported in the committee and would not have anything to do with discrediting that splendid piece of legislation.
Today, I heard the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Neale) say that the workers of Canada look upon this as the best unemployment insurance legislation in the world. It may be that he hashed an opportunity to talk to Harold Winch, the former member for Vancouver East who was a hard-working member of that committee and one who always looked after his responsibilities, particularly in respect of the working man. It seems to me that the new member for Vancouver East, although he may not be quite as eloquent as Mr. Winch because he has not had the same years of experience, certainly is putting forward the views of the working man. The working man in Canada today says that this is the best unemployment insurance scheme in the world. That is not to say that it is perfect. However, the government has recognized that it has a responsibility to the unemployed people to do what they can for them when they are in this particular predicament.
I listened to the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander) when he indicated that the government did not seem to care about unemployment. It always seems that the members of the opposition ignore the fact we have the fastest growing labour force in the world. Also they seem to forget conveniently the number of jobs which have been created while this party has been in
power. It is not a record of which we need be ashamed. I shall not quote all the statistics. Members of the opposition are very good at playing with figures in this field. I would just like to say that when they look at a glass of water they always seem to see it as 6 per cent empty rather than 94 per cent full. If you consider full employment to be at the level of 3 per cent unemployment, then 97 per cent of the people of Canada who want to work would be working.
So, the record is not as good as it should be, but it certainly is not as bad as members of the opposition would have us believe. That is why I support programs such as the LIP program which some people seem to knock as being against the work ethic. People, in effect, are doing their own thing. They are working at things they wish to work on or are working on something that is to the benefit of their community. This reminds me of the members of the Chippewa Indian reservation in my riding. They sought and obtained a LIP grant to do work on their own reservation. This gave them an opportunity to do things for their own benefit. It gave them a measure of dignity and enabled them to get away from employment which they did not particularly like in some areas. They were able in this way to work at home with their own people on the reservation. This gave dignity to the hard working Chippewa people on the reservation in my area of Sarnia. There is an obligation to protect the unemployed. That is why I think members of all parties today have spoken on behalf of the unemployment insurance plan.
Certainly there are improvements to be made and I think the hon. member for Vancouver East suggested some with which I could agree. I can think of other areas that should be looked at, quite frankly, in more depth. In the heat of the election battle a suggestion was being made by the Conservatives that the qualifying period should be increased from eight weeks to twelve weeks because the plan was being terribly abused. Before climbing on that bandwagon I thought I should check the facts. This was the irresponsible position taken by members of the Official Opposition until they came back here and found that there was little abuse in this area and that if we increased the qualifying period from eight to 12 weeks it would work to the detriment of the people in the Maritime region. I wonder whether the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) made that particular speech about increasing the qualifying period when he was speaking in his home base.
The other people to whom we have a responsibility are the students who are unemployed. Admittedly, they are unemployed only during a short period of time, but they do need money in order to finance their education. So, the government participates in student loan plans; it has put forward Opportunities for Youth programs, and the Department of National Defence offers a whole series of opportunities for young people to work. These programs do not put all young people to work, but they certainly create the right atmosphere and provide many jobs. It should be noted also that 50 per cent of the cost of post secondary education is taken care of by the federal government.

March 12, 1973

Then, there is the excellent on-the-job training plan. I was grieved to hear that all of the money in that particular program had not been utilized. I would like to suggest one amendment to the minister. I understand that students coming from school cannot qualify for this program unless they have been out of school at least a year. It seems to me that this is self-defeating. If a student can get on-the-job training, as many of them can, immediately upon leaving school, we should make this possible for him by spending some of the money available to make this a better plan.
Contrary to what the hon. member for Hamilton West said, nobody is playing with the work ethic. The situation is that this is a social question. A man works a good portion of his life to train for a particular job and then he is laid off from it. Should we then say to him: "you have to go back to being a labourer or to driving a truck" when he is training in a particular field? It is difficult for him to take that action. If there were no unemployment scheme or plan available to him, that is what he would do, he would take whatever job is available, but in this day and age, given the splendid buoyancy of our economy, I wonder if that is what we want to do to the working people who have achieved a certain measure of excellence in a particular field. Should they not have an opportunity to get back to their job and not have to take whatever is handed out at that time?
There is another complaint that comes from time to time, and that is that people in industries, such as the tobacco industry, cannot get people to work for them because of the temporary aspect of the job and the difficulty of the work. Also, this has an impact on the benefits people engaged in this type of employment received under the unemployment insurance scheme. It seems to me that we should take a look at this area because if an individual takes a job when he is drawing unemployment insurance, he takes it knowing at the outset that it will be temporary. Perhaps when he finishes that temporary job, the unemployment insurance benefits should be continued and he should be paid at the same rate he was paid before he took the job. Perhaps there is an amendment to the Unemployment Insurance Act that could be made so that people will be encouraged to take temporary jobs, and so that such employment will not work to their detriment so far as benefits under unemployment insurance are concerned.
Almost daily now you can pick up newspapers and find that municipalities are indicating that their welfare costs have gone down. This is precisely what was predicted by the former minister of labour when he was in this portfolio and afterwards; in effect, through the unemployment insurance scheme, we are giving people dignity. It is an insurance plan for which they paid a premium and they have a right to collect insurance benefits. We are, thereby taking them off welfare rolls. Locally, the municipality of Ottawa-Carleton has indicated that it did not use up its full budget on welfare last year and in fact is reducing it this year even more. I suspect this is a direct result of the splendid unemployment insurance scheme which is giving dignity to people and taking them off the welfare rolls.
Unemployment
Industry and, probably more correctly, unions recognized long before government that when people are, in permanent employment-and I am thinking primarily of the auto industry-and it becomes necessary to change over to new models which entails some tooling up or some machinery to be put in place, that TAB and supplementary insurance benefits should be provided. As a result, individuals will come back to work when the industry is prepared to put them back into full time labour. Thus, they are not laid off by that industry and they are taken care of during the change over period.
One thing which is of concern to me in the unemployment insurance scheme is the cheaters who abuse the plan. I think that we are unanimous throughout the House in our view of them. We can get all party agreement on that, I think. Perhaps we cannot get all party agreement on how ws should deal with this problem, but I think one of the messages that we have to put across to the Canadian public, and particularly to those who are paying into the unemployment insurance fund, is that they are the ones who are being cheated by those who abuse the plan. The people they should blame are the cheaters who abuse the plan, not the government which brought in the plan in the first place. Of course, we want to deal with people in a compassionate way, and we do not want to offend those who have paid into the plan and who are legitimately entitled to the unemployment insurance benefits. If some of these people suffer, it is unfortunate, but the blame should be placed more appropriately on the cheaters who abuse the plan and not on the government or on the officials who have the responsibility of administering the plan.
With regard to the unemployed, we have introduced legislation which makes provision, where significant layoffs take place as a result of technological change, for the collective bargaining agreement to be opened. There are all kinds of safeguards built in so that industry does not have to worry that technological change will have the effect of laying off a significant number of people. I do not think industry is bargaining in good faith with employees' representatives when it knows it will be bringing in technological change which will have the effect of laying off a significant number of people, yet it says, "yes, we will increase your wages by a certain percentage" knowing full well that not only will 400 or 500 people not collect that increase, they will not be collecting any salary or wages at all. I do not think that this is bargaining in good faith. If we have avoided that situation, then I think we have done a good job.
The hon. member for Hamilton West indicated that he deplored the unemployment situation, as his party has been doing for four and a half years. I would say amen to that; we all do. But what we have been waiting for in vain is for some measures that would be advocated by the official opposition to attack our number one problem. What we hear from the opposition is that the budget is not expansionary enough. The hon. member for Saint-Hyacin-the (Mr. Wagner) in on the record as indicating that the deficit should be in the neighbourhood of $4 billion. This moved the London Free Press to comment that probably he was put into external affairs to get him as far away as possible from the finance portfolio.
