speechtext:
The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Laprise:
That this House deplores the continuous increase in unemployment, as well as the refusal or negligence of the Government to propose effective measures for providing more jobs of a remunerative character for Canadians, and condemns the existing authorities for imposing or tolerating quasi-repressive measures affecting citizens who merely want to see respected their fundamental right to a decent standard of living and their personal dignity and to live in a climate of freedom and security.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-GOVERNMENT FAILURE RESPECTING NEGLIGENCE OF UNEMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the hon. member for Abitibi (Mr. Laprise) introduced this motion, some other hon. members felt he was getting away from the subject of this motion.
Mr. Speaker, I wish to emphasize that, not only did the hon. member for Abitibi not stray from the subject of his motion, but, on the contrary, he dealt with an essential aspect of that motion. In fact, not only is it important to blame the government for not taking adequate measures to stop increasing unemployment but we must also find out in what way this goal could be achieved.
March 12, 1973

In order to find the most appropriate means to this end, we must have a thorough knowledge of the real causes of this major problem, unemployment. All governments have had to face this problem for years and we will recall the time when the Progressive Conservative party was in office-this is not so long ago-when unemployment reached an unprecedented rate. It is therefore obvious that this is a permanent problem, and that despite all efforts that are made, it will never be solved. One does not need to be extremely clever to realize that if we fail to find any solution, it is only because we do not study thoroughly enough the major causes of unemployment.
This is why my hon. colleague from Abitibi has insisted on these major causes. In a society such as ours, where progress has been so far reaching, we must admit that all inventions which facilitate production increase unemployment. This matter has been raised for many years, and the Social Credit party has been most concerned to take the lead in this field, in order to forecast what is happening today.
As a matter of fact, whether we want it or not, we will one day be compelled to apply the basic principles that were put forward by Major C. H. Douglas, in the third issue of "Warning Democracy", and I quote:
Now, if you will consider the fact that the general output of goods of all descriptions per unit of mechanical labour employed, and that this energy has increased in the last 100 years by at least 3,000 to 4,000 per cent, you will see that one of three things must happen. Either everyone must consume thirty or forty times as much as he did before, and increase the amount as the amount of energy put into production increases, or (2) we must get rid, by exportation or otherwise, of an increasing amount of production, or (3) we must recognise that the so-called unemployment problem is something which arises out of the advancement of science applied to industry, and we must modify profoundly our system of distribution.
This is a denunciation of the main reason for unemployment. Once we have recognized the fact that income is one thing and salary another, since the development of society so requires, and when we have finally recognized that this distinction should be translated into adequate laws which would admit for instance that income does not exclusively mean salary, we shall have recognized at the same time that concessions should be made in a developed country such as ours where raw materials are plentyful and whose population is willing to produce.
In such a country each citizen who contributes to the material, spiritual and moral progress of our community should benefit from our wealth and enormous production.
To this end, the only means to obtain social justice is to guarantee to each Canadian a minimum income independently from his salary. At the same time we shall have made a reform which will encourage each individual to further improve his services to society and mainly his direct participation to production.
This is a basic principle and until it is understood no adequate solution will ever be found to unemployment. Under the current system in which we have to flounder to find remedies to the immediate consequences of unemployment, it is of course a problem involving all categories of our societies and which might cause still more troubles.
Unemployment
I should like to quote two paragraphs from an article published in the December 1972 edition of the publication Le Quebec industriel, and entitled The Scandal of Fake Unemployment-The Underlying Causes". I think that article gives a fairly clear idea of the problem being dealt with today, and I quote:
The campaign launched last November by LE QUEBEC INDUSTRIEL against fake unemployment practices has caused many a reaction-extremely favourable for the most part-from all political and economic circles.
It seems that the problem is a matter of concern to all classes of society, from the worker who has to pay with his deductions for the inadequacies of the system, to the businessmen who have to do without the required manpower and to the politicians who view with alarm the disastrous results of this government's generous, confusing and uncontrolled policy.
Mr. Speaker, such are in brief the conditions that evidently do prevail now and not merely because the Creditistes say so. Why? Because, as I have just said, this has not been provided for, and although it does favour a certain number of people who are consistenly trying to cheat the government in one way or another, I am convinced that there are only a few of them. Besides, as stated elsewhere in the article quoted agove, the number of people who manage to chisel certainly do not exceed 3 to 5 per cent.
Unfortunately a great number of honest workers are being frustrated because of the implementation of a legislation that had been heralded as being a lot more liberal than the former one-I say "liberal" not in the political sense of the word but in the true sense of the word itself- a legislation that would make unemployment insurance benefits more accessible to unemployed people.
Everybody seemed to be pleased, but looking at the effects of that legislation, we are compelled to say that it is almost a disaster, because our offices are swamped with unemployment insurance problems. Dozens of people come daily to ask us to intervene and help them obtain their benefits. Most of them, as I say, are honest workers who for one reason or another, are unemployed at a certain time. Since the legislation seems to be helpful to the workers under the circumstances, why are officials trying by all possible means to discourage if not to get rid of those benefit claimants? This is due to several reasons, especially because no distinction can be made between the swindler, the deceiver and the one who is caught in an unpleasant situation.
None the less, such a distinction can readily be made, Mr. Speaker. For instance, the man who has never collected unemployment insurance benefits is quite honest of course when he applies for benefits. Of course, being used to working every week, to getting his salary each weekend, when he has to wait for one, two or three months, and sometimes much longer, he suffers flagrant injustice. The trouble is, among other things, out and out centralization carried out inside the Unemployment Insurance Commission, and for the province of Quebec as a whole the operations are being performed in Montreal, which results not only in delays and errors, but also in injustice.
Therefore, it is most important that the government should consider this change; in other words, decentralization of the Unemployment Insurance Commission should

March 12, 1973
Unemployment
be considered with a view to having the local offices of the Commission receive, study, and process the claims.
Mr. Speaker, the officials of the Trois-Rivieres office being closer to the workers in that area, they no doubt are in a better position to study with more speed the problems involved in an unemployment insurance claim, and consequently, to have it processed in a sounder, more logical and more equitable fashion.
This matter is becoming sensitive on account of the unlimited problems involved. If a worker has to wait for weeks and months, he nevertheless has to keep alive. And for this, he must accept either to get into debt or to go begging for social welfare allowances.
As we know, Mr. Speaker, it is not pleasant to go and beg for benefits from the welfare people. Anyhow, the request must still be considered for one month, and then difficulties are made concerning the payment to be granted. In other words, we are considerably complicating the life of the worker and particularly when he is the head of a family.
Mr. Speaker, if unemployment is accepted, since nobody yet seems prepared to make a thorough review of this foolish system in which we are struggling, the law should be administered as it stands, and nothing should be done to needlessly frustrate workers with all sorts of more or less coercive procedures. This is what we are condemning in our motion, Mr. Speaker. We are condemning the authorities who impose or tolerate some almost repressive measures.
When an individual suddenly falls ill while working and must, lacking any other resources, fall back on unemployment insurance, it is a denial of his rights to require repeated submission of medical reports describing his illness and stipulating a date for his recovery.
Mr. Speaker, it seems quite normal to intensify control of possible fraud. Fraud might well exist in some cases. In the vast majority of cases, when a worker has to stop work and therefore consults a doctor who clearly indicates that the state of his health precludes working in the immediate or near future, why create all kinds of problems for him? Actually, in cases of illness, and I have in mind more specifically a nervous breakdown, it is very difficult to determine when the individual will be able to return to work. It is quite difficult to determine, even by a doctor. A date is then set arbitrarily. In my opinion, we should at least give the doctor the benefit of the doubt and accept the fact that his diagnosis constitutes sufficient proof of entitlement to unemployment insurance benefits.
Mr. Speaker, to be precise I must say that there are various ways of fighting unemployment. For a few years now the government, through local initiative projects or through the Opportunities for Youth Program has succeeded in creating new jobs. Of course, such projects may not have given the desired results and for this reason we should, as a matter of fact, think of improving them, of carrying out other kinds of projects.
Having noticed some deficiency in this regard, I wonder, for instance, if priority should not be given to local initiatives projects for which the names of unemployed willing to work have already been submitted. If 10 or 15 unemployed, thanks to their initiative or that of others in their community, give their names to work on a project, they should be given priority so that we might no longer see, as we have in the past, projects approved but not completed for lack of workers. That is just one incidental suggestion.
There are many other ways of fighting unemployment. The millions of dollars paid out in unemployment insurance benefits could instead be used to create jobs. Unemployment could be reduced, for instance, if municipalities were allowed new credits, interest free as much as possible, in order to get work done, not only to give people work, but also to meet essential needs.
In this way, one would not have to make it a condition that it be done in the winter months, for the problem for the potentially unemployed is knowing whether to continue out of work or to go and work just for a month or two for an income that is about the same as the unemployment benefit. Faced with this kind of a dilemma, despite their finer feelings, the unemployed prefer to keep warm near the stove than to go and freeze in sub-zero temperatures. There can be no doubt about that! Let us not confront the work with such an impossible choice.
For these reasons, we ought to provide municipalities, for example, with sufficient funds for them to have essential work done. What municipality does not have work that needs to be done? In this way they could wipe out unemployment and help us to make some progress until there is a complete reform of this system that incorporates permanent unemployment.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-GOVERNMENT FAILURE RESPECTING NEGLIGENCE OF UNEMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
First of all, Mr. Speaker, I wish to indicate the portion of the resolution to which I intend to address my remarks. It is that part which-
-condemns the existing authorities for imposing or tolerating quasi-repressive measures affecting citizens who merely want to see respected their fundamental right to a decent standard of living and their personal dignity and to live in a climate of freedom and security.
I appreciate the opportunity to take part in this debate. The subject is most timely, bearing in mind the situation in which many of the unemployed in the rural areas which I represent find themselves at the present time. I am glad to participate for two reasons. First, it gives me an opportunity to speak out on behalf of seasonal agricultural workers in the Norfolk-Haldimand area. This is an intensive cash crop area. It is a highly labour-intensive area. Labour is used only at the peak season of the year- the harvest season. Perhaps in Norfolk-Haldimand there is a greater concentration of seasonal workers than exists anywhere else in Canada. Certainly, the concentration is as great.
These workers are being deliberately and systematically disentitled from receiving unemployment insurance benefits. This action is being taken on a wholesale basis. When I asked whether it was the policy of the Commission to disentitle these people, the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Andras) said, in response to my question the other day as reported in Hansard at page 1636:

March 12, 1973

"Absolutely no. Not as such." Then he went on to say that they could be disentitled in certain circumstances. I propose to deal with this answer later. I am speaking, now, about the large class of workers in my area who are being disentitled for entirely the wrong reason.
My second reason for rising to speak today on the motion before us is this: I want to explain more fully the terms "Gestapo tactics" which I used when I was speaking about the activities of benefit control officers in my area. What I said in the House on that occasion will be found reported in Hansard on the same page I mentioned earlier.
Several hundred additional control officers were hired by the Unemployment Insurance Commission recently to cut out the cheats and chisellers who wrongfully obtained benefits under the act. Such people have increased the cost of unemployment insurance-a cost which has already been brought home dramatically to the government by resolutions in this chamber and by debates in the House. All hon. members are aware that the Commission has overspent, that it has gone beyond the ceiling set in the original act. Bill C-124 was brought down not long ago to remove the ceiling. Thus, the government was doubly anxious to cut the cost of unemployment insurance. It appears to me, though, that in its effort to cut costs the Commission has approached the subject in the wrong way. It is right and proper that control officers should be appointed and that they should carry out proper investigative procedures to cut out cheats and chisellers. There is no quarrel with that proposition. However, in a rural area such as I represent, the timing was most unfortunate.
In spite of what the hon. member for Sarnia-Lambton (Mr. Cullen) said a few minutes ago, I feel, too, that the time required for the securing of benefits by these agricultural workers is far too short. I am referring to the eight week period. There are those in my area who worked during the tobacco harvest. They worked for eight weeks, enough to qualify them for unemployment insurance benefits, and then they refused to work longer. It is at this point benefit control officers should have intervened. As a result of the refusal of these people to continue employment, apples in the orchards of Norfolk County were left on trees as winter approached. These men and women could not be induced to leave their unemployment insurance benefits and go out into the fields and orchards to work. This is the time the control officers should have been on the job.
In my area at the present time there is obviously no farm help required. There are very few small industries in the towns and villages in the area. As far as help is concerned, these plants are all filled to capacity. They do not want any more help. As a matter of fact, some are laying off employees. The benefit control officers are coming in and cutting these people off unemployment insurance, saying they are not looking for a job.
I wish to go into some detail with regard to the procedures used to disentitle persons properly entitled to benefits. First, the individual who is receiving the claim is interviewed. He then receives a letter of disentitlement setting out the reasons he is being disentitled. I can recite
Unemployment
these reasons because I have heard them hundreds of times from people who have complained to me about the actions of these men. First, they are told that they really do not want to work; second, there are no child care arrangements and, third, they do not have any visible means of transportation. This occurs over and over again. When a person telephones me, I know exactly what will be in the letter he is going to read to me. Included with the letter of disentitlement is a slip that states that person has 30 days in which to appeal the case. In order to appeal, the claimant must write a letter setting out the reason he is appealing, the reason he is refuting the grounds for disentitlement which are stated in the letter.
The case is heard by a board of referees. This board is to include a representative of labour, representative of management and a representative of the Unemployment Insurance Commission. In all the cases that have ever come to my attention, and this runs into many hundreds, not once has this board of referees reversed the original decision of the benefit control officer. It is a folly, a cruel joke on the people to say they have a right to appeal. To add insult to injury, these people are advised that they have a right to appeal to an umpire. The only way to do that is to obtain permission to appeal to the umpire. If the decision is unanimous, which it always is, there is no right to appeal to an umpire, a judge, one who truly would not have a vested interest in the decision. This is a cruel joke, deliberately being played on these people.
That is not the basic complaint of the people in my area. It is the tactics used by the interviewing officer when claimants are being interrogated. These officers first ask if the claimant is looking for work. The person replies that he has registered with Manpower. Manpower, if it is to mean anything at all, should be the agency which puts people in touch with jobs. If jobs are available, Manpower should advise the person. Surely, that is sufficient evidence that an individual is looking for work.
If a person decides to appeal, he telephones the farmers in the area, knowing full well that they have no employment at this time of the year. He calls them because this is where he worked. If he worked for an industry, he calls the plant, knowing full well that this plant does not need extra employees. As I said, some industries are even laying off employees. These people are sick and tired of being continually asked, for work when everyone in the community knows there is none.
There is another trick which these officers play on these people being interviewed. When they enter a person's home and see small children, they ask whether that individual has a babysitter. Obviously, there is no babysitter because that person is home looking after the children. The honest answer is no. When the signed statement comes back, it states that the claimant has no child care arrangements and, therefore, is unable to accept work if suitable work were offered. How dishonest can you get?
Another trick is with regard to transportation. The individual is asked whether he has a car. Perhaps the husband has a car but the wife has not. There is one car for the family. The officer does not say to the wife, if a job were offered in Simcoe, Delhi or on a nearby farm, could you get to work? The answer would be entirely different. These people are scared out of their wits when a govern-

March 12, 1973
Unemployment
ment investigator comes to the door. They will sign almost anything to get rid of him. The signed statement is then used before the board of referees. It is about this that I complain most bitterly. I did not have time to elaborate on this in the House a few weeks back. These are the types of things that I refer to as gestapo tactics.
Many of the seasonal workers who are unemployed are new Canadians. They are of different ethnic origins. Many came to this country from central European countries. They are older people. They did not have the opportunity nor the ability to become conversant in English. They can speak it passably, but they cannot understand it very well. They certainly cannot read or write English. The officers take advantage of them by getting them to sign a document about which they know nothing.
I agree with the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Neale) that this type of tactic is wrong. Surely there are honest and correct ways of weeding out those who should be taken off the unemployment insurance payroll. This way is unworthy of a civilized government. The interrogator is a professional. He has been trained. He is pitting his wits and skill against people who are unskilled in English and have a marginal education. These people are scared to death when a government investigator comes to their door. These are some things that are wrong with the system being applied to seasonal agricultural workers. I wish to make a few general comments about the way this plan is being applied in my area. Many of the people who are being cut off from unemployment insurance benefits have no other means of subsistence. They must go to the local municipal welfare officer and ask to be placed on welfare. A few moments ago a member opposite said that unemployment insurance was a boon to the welfare system, that it would take people off welfare and lessen the bills of the municipality. In my area our welfare officers are hopping mad about the number of people being disqualified from legitimate unemployment insurance payments and being placed on welfare. This is wrong.
These people who are doing the investigating might well consult with the welfare officers in the area in which they are working. The welfare officers could tell them who the chiselers are and who is entitled to unemployment insurance benefits. These investigators are lacking in experience and do not have a knowledge of the community in which they are working. Why do they not contact someone who knows the situation and can guide them in a reasonable sort of way?
Another point I wish to emphasize is the unfortunate timing in the drive to cut people off benefits. Surely, the time to do this is when farmers and other employers are desperately seeking assistance for harvesting or whatever. This is the time we could determine who is unwilling to work. This is the time unemployment insurance control officers should be in the field doing their job.
Better still, these people should not have been placed on the rolls in the first place. Perhaps this is the most ironic part of it all. These people are casual workers who leave their homes and go to work harvesting farm crops, whether it be tobacco, orchard crops, asparagus or whatever it may be. They did not ask to be put on unemployment insurance in the first place. As a matter of fact, they

objected strenuously and so did the farmers who employed them. They did not want any part of it. They were willing to take their chances and get employment in the summertime during the harvest, which would have provided them with some money. But having been put on unemployment insurance and having made their contributions, they cannot for the life of them see why they are not justly entitled to the benefits for which they have paid.
Another matter that surprised me and caused a great deal of pain to some who have received unemployment insurance benefits, having had their claims allowed by the commission, is that suddenly, having received their cheques, they found they were disentitled to benefits. The Unemployment Insurance Commission then had the nerve to ask them to pay back the money they had received. Surely this tells us something about the system and the way it is being administered. Why in the world were these people paid benefits in the first place? These are some of the reasons I feel very upset, as do the people I represent-I am putting it mildly; they would use much stronger language-over the way unemployment insurance is being administered in my area.
In response to a question I asked the other day, the minister said that he would investigate cases in my area if I would give him specific instances. I have since flooded his office with these cases and I can send him many more. As a matter of fact, the people in my constituency are writing directly to the minister, so he need not worry about not having enough cases to investigate. Literally hundreds of workers have written, phoned or spoken to me about this matter. They cannot understand this system under which they have contributed and thus feel justly entitled to benefits. They have been honest and straightforward in answering questions put to them, but when they are tricked into disqualifying themselves they surely have the right to get mad.
Farmers are also deeply disturbed because this type of worker is being disentitled. They fear, and have good reason to fear, that next year no one will bother finding work at harvest time because they fear deductions will be made from their wages and they will get nothing in return. The farmers think that the farm labour situation next harvest season will be aggravated by this situation.
One positive note. I have been critical all the way through my remarks, but I feel that much of this would never have happened had the government not divorced Manpower from unemployment insurance. Surely if Manpower and unemployment were lumped together under the one administration, Manpower would know right on the spot who was available for work and entitled to receive an unemployment insurance cheque.
I suggest a return to the system where cheques are distributed at the Manpower centre, where the recipient will pick them up. If it is more efficient to have the cheque prepared by a cheque-writing machine in Belleville, or wherever it may be, then let that be done. But do not distribute the cheques through the mails; let the local Manpower centre distribute them. They are on the spot and they know the situation. If a person is entitled to a cheque, he will receive it. If there is a job available for
March 12, 1973

him, he takes the job and does not get the cheque. That would soon clear up this whole mess.
Secondly, as I have already mentioned in my remarks, the investigating officers-the benefit control officers, as they are called-would be well advised to be a little more humane and understanding in the way they conduct their interrogations. Why not let claimants go to the welfare officer in the community, or a person such as a municipal councillor or clerk? They know the situation. They know the people who are in need of and are entitled to benefits. They also know the chisellers who would rather sit back and receive a hand-out from the government.
Those are the remarks I have to present for the consideration of the government. Hopefully, we will get some action to clear up this very serious and aggravating unemployment insurance situation in the area I represent.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-GOVERNMENT FAILURE RESPECTING NEGLIGENCE OF UNEMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) introduced his budget almost one month ago he began his address by saying, as reported at page 1428 of Hansard:
Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this budget is-first and foremost- to bring about a substantial reduction in unemployment. Unemployment is much more than an economic problem.
Then he said:
This budget is aimed at the faster growth of our economy and the strengthening of its basic structure in order to achieve the greatest possible increase in the number of permanent, satisfying jobs for our rapidly growing labour force.
Those phrases had a familiar ring, Mr. Speaker. I turned to the first speech of the Minister of Finance following his appointment to that office almost one year ago. On February 24, 1972, he said:
Our most urgent and pressing task is to bring about a substantial reduction in the level of unemployment. Our goal, our objective, must be the provision of a job to every Canadian who is seeking work.
They are very fine words, Mr. Speaker. However, if one looks not at the words but at the actions, one sees that the minister has been a complete failure; because when the minister took on the job of Minister of Finance in February, 1972, the rate of unemployment at that time, as it had been for more than two years prior to that date, was over 6 per cent on a seasonally adjusted basis. In January, 1973, the last month for which we have figures, the rate df unemployment on a seasonally adjusted basis was still 6.2 per cent.
According to the Toronto Globe and Mail for February 7, 1973, the unemployment rate dropped to 6.2 per cent in January, from 6.7 per cent in December of 1972. The Globe and Mail goes on to say:
The actual proportion of the labour force without work last month was 7.7 per cent ... It compares with 7.7 per cent a year earlier, 8 per cent in January, 1971, and 6.1 per cent in January, 1970 . ..
The unadjusted number of unemployed was 688,000 in January, 1973, compared with 584,000 in December and 665,000 in January, 1972.
In other words, there were 23,000 more people unemployed in January of 1973 than there were in January, 1972. If you look at the regional breakdown, Mr. Speaker, you will find there were more people unemployed in the Atlantic provinces in January of 1973 than there were in
Unemployment
January of 1972. That was also the case in Quebec, on the Prairies and in British Columbia. The only province in which there was a slight reduction in unemployment was Ontario.
Under those circumstances it is no wonder that the election of October, 1972, led to such a sharp reduction in the number of Liberal Members of Parliament. We had been telling the government, particularly the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the Minister of Finance, that unemployment was an important matter to the people of Canada. We had been saying that for over two years. For almost three years we have been told that the real problem is not unemployment but the rapid increase in the cost of living.
No country in the western world, with the exception of the United States, has a higher percentage of unemployment than Canada. This Minister of Finance, like the previous minister, says all the right things. He says that his objective is to reduce the number of unemployed and to provide jobs for every person in Canada who wants to work. But to put it mildly, I have been dismayed by the talk in Ottawa among senior civil servants in both the Department of Finance and the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce. They believe that in fact we have virtually full employment. There may be full employment for all the economists working for the government, but there is certainly not full employment for people who want to work in factories; and there certainly is not full employment or the prospect of anything near full employment for the young people who will be graduating from universities across Canada this year or coming out of community colleges in the next couple of months.
The figures we were given for the month of January show that 11.2 per cent of all workers between the age of 14 and 24 were unemployed. That is the situation, and the people of Canada are again being sold a bill of goods. Let me say to the government that the people of Canada did not believe them in October, 1972, they believed them less in February, 1973, and they will believe them even less in months to come.
All the projections of independent economists indicate that the reduction in the percentage of unemployment will be very small in the next four or five months and indicate that in the fall of 1973 unemployment in total numbers and in terms of percentage will begin to rise again. These are the projections of independent economists, not of those who work in the Department of Finance who have been preconditioned by the deputy minister not to tell the minister what they really think or to give him their real estimates.
That is the record of this Liberal government which has been in power since 1968. The percentage of unemployment this country has suffered since the present Prime Minister has been in office is almost twice as large as the unemployment we had under the previous prime minister. It is almost as large, although not quite, as the percentage we had under a Conservative government from 1957 to 1962.
We said we would support the budget debate, and we did, because it moved forward in certain directions. It

March 12, 1973
Unemployment
contained improvements to old age pensions which were fairly substantial although far short of what we wanted. We believed basic pensions should have been increased to $150 per month and we thought a beginning should have been made to lower the age at which individuals were eligible to receive the pension. We felt that if we gave people of age 60 and up an opportunity to retire on a voluntary basis, many of them would do so, leaving openings for young, unemployed people. In any event, we thought the increase to $100 a month was an improvement.
We felt that the income tax cut was not only an improvement but an expansionary measure. The $100 minimum reduction in income tax meant that many workers and farmers in low income brackets would in fact have a reduction of income tax up to 40 per cent, and we welcomed that. Let me say to the Minister of Finance and members of the government that in the opinion of economists of provincial and federal governments, as well as academic economists, this budget and the proposals of the government will fall far short of providing the kind of stimulus required to put the unemployed to work. It has been suggested by some of the best economists in the country that this budget is not nearly as expansionary as the budget presented by the minister in May, 1972, yet that budget did nothing at all to reduce unemployment.
The increase in the basic old age pension and the income tax cut, particularly for those in the lower income brackets, was a welcome step in the right direction. Both socially and in terms of justice, these changes go part way at least in meeting the criticisms of the budgets of the Liberals and Conservatives over the years. The latest budget will not do those expansionary things the Minister of Finance has suggested it will do. It will not reduce unemployment.
What should be done? We have said over the years that a number of things must be done. First of all, the secrecy about what this government thinks is likely to happen in terms of unemployment should come to an end. We cannot deal with the problems of unemployment when the people of Canada do not know what is likely to take place in the next year. The federal government cannot work out plans in co-operation with the provinces and the municipalities if it keeps secret the estimates of its own advisers economists and statisticians. The first thing this government ought to do is make public the projections made for it by its various departments and agencies as to the percentage of unemployment which is likely to exist in the coming year. This information should be made public on a quarterly basis. Once this has been done the federal government could work out, in co-operation with the provinces and municipalities, tri-level plans and projects to put people back to work. There are numerous projects that have not yet been attempted in this country.
One solution to unemployment was referred to earlier this afternoon by the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Basford). He introduced proposed amendments to the National Housing Act. We need a massive acceleration in the provision of housing accommodation for people in low income and middle income brackets. People can no longer afford to buy homes in cities like Toronto, because of what has happened to housing costs. Not only low

income people, but families in the middle income bracket can no longer afford to purchase homes. We need a massive attack in the field of housing to provide the required accommodation.
I note that the Minister of State for Science and Technology (Mrs. Sauve) is in the House. We must do something about pollution. I wish I could say that the city of Montreal had begun to do something about this problem, but one fact is that the vast majority, if not all of its raw sewage is still being dumped, untreated, into the St. Lawrence River. We can help the city of Montreal put on the Olympic games in 1976, but we cannot help it do something about the pollution situation in the St. Lawrence River which has existed for years. This is an indication of the stupidity of the Liberal government. I wish we could do something about meeting the educational and recreational needs of the people of this country. These facilities are deficient in many ways. These are some of the things in which governments could become involved.
Having said some good things about the budget, let me say that I believe that if we really want to put the people of Canada to work and reduce the number of unemployed, if we want by January 1, 1974, instead of 678,000 unemployed to have only 400,000 unemployed, the best way to do this would be to put money into the pockets of the people in the low income bracket. They would spend every penny of it. I suggest to the Minister of Finance and to the government that the $100 basic pension simply is not enough.
If we increased the basic pension to $125 a month, 99 per cent of the old age pensioners would spend every extra dollar given to them. In this way we could provide employment for thousands of unemployed people. Instead of the $100 minimum reduction in income tax, the reduction should have been a minimum of $135. Had all this been done we would really have an expansionary budget and a deficit of $1 billion more than the projected deficit the Minister of Finance has put forward which is not nearly expansionary enough.
Let me close by saying to the government that in recent years we have had something new in Canadian parliamentary life. We have had in recent years two budgets rather than one. I suggest to the Minister of Finance that the budget he has proposed is not expansionary enough and in the next three months the number of unemployed will not drop sharply as he suggested. In this event, we insist, on the basis of past experience and the estimates we have made, that the minister should do one of the things the former minister of finance did. There was at least one example of pioneering by the former minister. If the present Minister of Finance would follow that precedent, three or four months from now he would bring forward another budget which would be really expansionary and would bring the unemployed people of Canada back to work, which is where they really want to be.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-GOVERNMENT FAILURE RESPECTING NEGLIGENCE OF UNEMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I begin by apologizing for my absence this afternoon and therefore my inability to have noted all the comments of previous speakers. The inclement weather today forced me to drive this afternoon. I ask hon. members to please forgive my comments if they do not deal with all the particular points previous speakers have raised. Certainly, in reading Hansard I digest any comment that has been made, take the advice offered and do what I can with it.
The subject matter of the resolution indicates the continuing concern for Canada's serious unemployment situation which is no less grave, of course, because it remains puzzling and frustrating in the context of our generally buoyant economic conditions. As has been stated and in fact should be restated, part of our problem is demographic. We are still trying to cope with the Canadian phenomenon which is the fastest growing labour force among the industrialized nations, for which there are two main reasons.
The first reason is the post-war birth rate, and the second the fact that women among our society are increasingly taking part in work opportunities and in fact their participation still remains lower, as a percentage of the total population, than in some other countries. So I think we can anticipate both these problems being with us for some years to come, which indeed makes it even more necessary that we cope with them.
Our job creation rate for these new workers has been good: it has been improving. But I know all members of the House on all sides would like to see this general problem solved. I note the resolution states that "this House deplores the continuous increase in unemployment." I think, in all fairness and to place the facts before hon. members, we must note that the unemployment rate has been declining since last September; employment has been climbing every month with the exception of December.

speechtext:
This is in no small way due to the measures that have been taken for some time, beginning with our expansionary budgets back in 1970. Referring again to the budget of May 1972, I draw attention also to the early fall
Unemployment
announcement of some $80 million for the Local Initiatives Program which was bolstered by a major announcement by my colleague, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner), and myself on December 6 regarding $500 million for a direct employment program. This included an additional $80 million for the Local Initiatives Program to bring that to $165 million, and $10 million more for the on-the-job training program to increase that to $50 million. There was also a $350 million special municipal loan fund to be spread over the next three years, and other measures described in the announcement to which I have referred. These measures were topped on February 19 last by another expansionary budget of the Minister of Finance which contained massive tax cuts which will provide more income for spending, particularly oriented toward families in the lower income brackets.
Unemployment rates have been going down steadily since September. Very shortly we will have the February figures and I think we can expect to see further improvements in them. During the last several days the budget measures have been debated at length and I do not think I would be contributing to this debate were I to rehash the statements of the Minister of Finance and other colleagues. I would, therefore, like to take this opportunity to concentrate more on my responsibilities, namely, manpower and manpower programs.
This evening I would like to outline in particular our four-part program related to providing jobs and some of the special efforts we shall be making on behalf of the youth of this country, women, our native peoples and others who are disadvantaged. My comments may take me a little past the time allotted for my speech, in which case I would be most grateful if the House would permit me to complete my remarks so they would have continuity and totality.
Our jobs program will contain four elements: job finding, job creation, the elimination of artificial job barriers, and improved job satisfaction or job enrichment. First, we want much more comprehensive and efficient jobfinding techniques and services which will aggressively search out jobs and match them with the people available for work. Where we cannot make such a match, it is our intention to focus more clearly and bring into play our training, our mobility and our immigration policies and programs. At the very heart of this job-finding service will be an open, self-service job information centre where people who are ready to take a job will be put in touch with job data with an absolute minimum of red tape and bureaucracy.
Two such pilot projects have been announced and started recently, one in the national capital, Ottawa, and the other in Hamilton. This type of open, self-service job information centre will be the key, also, to a new relationship between Manpower and Unemployment Insurance Commission offices which we hope will ensure maximum utilization of available jobs and minimum delay in filling them. A co-operative working relationship now exists between these two agencies, Manpower and Immigration and the UIC, and it is being further developed. I think this will greatly facilitate the work of both and improve services to the public.

March 12, 1973
Unemp loyment
When workers apply lor unemployment insurance benefits they are now required to register for work with the Canada Manpower Centre if they are in need of CMC services. The only people excluded from this are those on short-term lay-offs, with definite knowledge that they will be recalled shortly, unless of course even for them there are vacancies known in the CMC offices that they could fill.
As it stands now, all Canada Manpower Centres supply the Unemployment Insurance Commission with lists of current vacancies for which they require workers, and persons applying for benefits who have the skills are required to report to the CMC within 24 hours. As an example of the effect of this, during the past three months in Quebec the UIC referred to the CMCs 3,228 workers, of whom 571 were immediately referred to employers. From the benefit control point of view, another 1,000 failed to report to the CMCs and the UIC was notified for investigation of possible disqualification, and the CMCs notified the UIC of another 472 cases requiring similar investigation.
Canada Manpower Centres thus have access to all claimants of unemployment insurance who are capable of working, and if a UIC claimant refuses offers of suitable employment the CMC notifies the commission. In fact, with that arrangement during the past nine months the CMCs have notified the commission of over 100,000 such cases. Further, CMCs provide a recall service to employers who are having difficulty locating former workers. This does happen from time to time. If these employees are not working and do not report for work, again the CMCs will notify the commission.
The co-operation between the Department of Manpower and Immigration and the Unemployment Insurance Commission is emphasized by these arrangements that have recently been made. In localities where there is no UIC office, the Canada Manpower Centres provide UIC services. They are staffed to assist claimants, either by providing space for UIC personnel or by having specially trained CMC personnel provide the UIC services.
Right now the UIC is represented in 144 Canada Manpower Centres. There is day to day contact between officials of the CMCs and the UIC concerning individuals, working out procedures and the exchange of information. At the regional level, both organizations have liaison officers and here in Ottawa there is an inter-agency committee of officials, co-chaired by assistant deputy ministers, to develop further operational relationships and co-ordination of activities that will ensure greater assistance to the unemployed.
But, Mr. Speaker, even after we have improved our utilization of existing job opportunities I am quite sure there will still, unfortunately, be gaps to fill and they probably can only be filled by direct job creation. The level of unemployment, due to the factor I outlined at the beginning of my comments, namely, the growth in the labour force, will continue to be a challenge to all of us. The economic measures announced by the Minister of Finance on several occasions no doubt will reduce unemployment. But even when unemployment rates return to more normal levels, our Canadian climate ensures that we will continue to have strong seasonal fluctuations in

employment levels. Moreover, Mr. Speaker, regardless of the season of the year, in good years and in bad some parts of Canada and some groups of Canadians will face particular unemployment problems throughout the 1970s and beyond. These employment problems, in all likelihood, will be complicated by rapidly changing job expectations and other social factors.
I am convinced that in addition to the indirect measures of fiscal and monetary policy open to us, and the stimulation of the private sector where the bulk of jobs must be created, we shall need well planned programs of direct job creation for some time to come. We have learned a lot in the last two or three years about direct job creation under OFY and the Local Initiatives Program and, as I announced recently, we are experimenting with this year's LIP in a number of ways. I would like to give the House some examples of this experimentation.
Wells, in British Columbia, is situated near the historic Cariboo Trail, four miles from Barkerville, a lively centre in the 1858 gold rush. Using Local Initiatives Program funds to employ local jobless, the Wells Improvement District is completing projects that will ensure more employment opportunities for local residents throughout the year. Another experiment is a project being run by the Indians of Lac LaHache, northern Saskatchewan, who rely almost totally on an annual ice harvest for their livelihood. This board recently applied to the Local Initiatives Program for support to ensure the completion of the harvest, and that experiment is under way. There are literally thousands of such projects under way in Canada. On the whole, the 1972-73 Local Initiatives Program will have created approximately 350,000 man-months of employment and about 85,000 jobs. As I have mentioned in the House previously, more than 5,860 projects have been approved.
The training-on-the-job program is another tool that has been used by my department to find work and to provide valuable training experience for the unemployed. Approximately 200,000 man-months of employment are being created this year, representing 60,000 jobs. This compares favourably with last year's effort when about 42,000 unemployed were hired by employers under a similar program.
I am also satisfied that many local initiative projects can become continuing, self-sufficient enterprises, selling their products or services without unfair competition to existing enterprises. We shall be working with many project sponsors to examine such possibilities in the next several months. In addition, as part of our new services for the disadvantaged we are developing, with several provinces, a number of experimental LIP type projects aimed at specific groups of the hard core unemployed. Such projects will last two or three years, not just a few months, and are intended not only to create jobs but to enable the workers to become conditioned to the world of work and to gain the self-confidence and self-reliance which come from accomplishment. Like LIP, the projects will be dependent on the initiative of citizens' groups, but the projects, known as local employment assistance projects-which no doubt will be called LEAP-will involve provinces and municipalities in their planning and implementation.
March 12, 1973

But more important than these specific initiatives and experiments, we feel that we must begin to put machinery in place that will, in concert with other government departments, with the provinces and business continually test and plan job creation schemes which we should have on the shelf to use when unemployment rises.
I think it will be clear from what I have said that I, too, am far from satisfied with Canada's historic band-aid approach to direct job creation. What is needed now is a longer term and better planned approach. In the immediate future, as far as my department is concerned, I think we have to face the following tasks: What are we to do with the Local Initiatives Program and the Opportunities for Youth program? How do we build on the good features and eliminate the bad ones?
Second, we must move now to establish the planning machinery. Third, we have to set in place, after putting before the House our suggestions, the new programs which are necessary. I shall be making recommendations to my colleagues soon on these very important matters.
For some people, no increase in new jobs will really help in the ordinary course of events because of the structural barriers between them and the jobs that exist. Some of these barriers have been identified and dealt with by the introduction of our training and mobility programs; others remain because employers in this country still tend to discriminate against candidates for work, though often unthinkingly, on grounds of age, sex, experience, race, pattern of previous employment and education.
It is in that context that we plan a series of positive measures to try to break through these structural barriers. First of all, in the area of education and persuasion, employers, including public employers, will be encouraged to base their hiring standards on the real performance objectives of the jobs, rather than on some of the artificial standards designed primarily to limit the workload of the recruiting officers. This will be greatly aided by the new Canadian Classification and Dictionary of Occupation which became available for my department on January 1, 1973.
In the area of placement incentives, under the Canada Manpower training-on-the-job program two new elements have been announced which will greatly facilitate job matching. The first is training on the job for skill shortages. Where an employer's job order cannot be filled by CMC from the existing work force for a period of 30 days or more, we shall offer to enter into a contract with that employer to train unqualified or underqualified workers to fill the need. As far as training on the job for the disadvantaged is concerned, in the case of the hard core disadvantaged employers will be offered reimbursement of up to 100 per cent of wages for an initial period to hire and retain disadvantaged workers.
The fourth element of our four-part jobs program relates to the growing phenomenon in this country, and I think in the whole western world, of worker dissatisfaction with the jobs facing them. There is little evidence to suggest that this is opposition to work itself but, rather, it appears to be a rebellion against certain types of work which are distasteful, undignified or lacking in personal
Unemployment
satisfaction. We know now that workers will sometimes accept relatively lower wages for satisfying work but will react against boring, repetitive work even at very high wages.
There is a need for extensive research and private and public sector co-operation in dealing with this problem. My department will offer co-operation to companies or industries encountering such labour problems identified in the main by high labour turnover. My department's capacity to provide this co-operation must surely be extended.
These are the main elements of our jobs program. However, I should also like to say a few words about several distinct groups of our Manpower clientele for whom special affirmative action is required and being developed- youth, women, native workers and disadvantaged workers generally. I should like to take this opportunity, Mr. Speaker, to announce a number of adjustments to manpower programs to provide better service to Canadian workers who are encountering particular difficulty in getting and holding jobs and who would continue to face that difficulty even if unemployment decreases as we hope it will.
In this next fiscal year, Mr. Speaker, we shall be making a modest start at least, and with experience we hope to build a real response to the employment needs of many Canadians who heretofore have existed on the fringes of the labour force, chronically or intermittently unemployed. The nature of our new services are described in a letter which my colleague, the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde), and I recently sent to the provincial welfare ministers and which I shall be tabling in the House later this week.
The highlights of this approach include, first, hiring and placing 110 specially trained counsellors in CMCs across Canada to specialize in the problems of workers with severe employment problems and to advise our regular Manpower counsellors on how to deal with such cases, as well as to provide a point of contact with community agencies offering other specialized services. Second, our CMCs will be given new authority and funds to refer clients to professional practitioners and diagnostic services when they have problems which extend beyond our internal resources. Third, major changes are being made to our Manpower training programs. We shall purchase work adjustment training from sheltered workshops or private employers to teach people how to work. We shall introduce basic literacy training. We shall adjust the so-called 52-week rule to permit greater flexibility in training durations for those with particular problems. We shall be adding what we call "life skills" components to the regular training program.
I saw a marvellous pilot project on this very matter in Windsor last week when I was visiting that city-the St. Clair Community College and Holy Rosary Recreation Centre. I would advise hon. members who have the opportunity to visit that experimental project; I am sure it will thrill them as it did me.
We shall be tailoring training programs more carefully to the needs of individuals, and planning longer term packages of training and work experience to bring disadvantaged workers to full employability. Fourth, we are

March 12, 1973
Unemployment
introducing a new training-on-the-job scheme in which disadvantaged workers will be placed in jobs, backed by counselling and supportive services. We expect this coming year to spend $10 million to $15 million on this element.
Fifth, we are expanding our outreach services to extend to workers with particular needs not easily met by normal CMC services. I will give an example of this. We have entered into a contract with the Metis Association of Alberta to hire Metis employment counsellors to work with our CMCs, to explain our services to the Metis, counsel them, place them in jobs and follow up this service. We intend to spend $2.6 million on similar projects next year in an experimental way.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, our local employment assistance program-LEAP-is at this stage a modest demonstration-type program designed to test longer term projects similar to LIP but aimed at specific groups of hard core unemployed. In addition to job creation and community betterment, these projects must involve the workers in a developmental process designed to lead them to full-time work and continuing self-sufficiency. It is our intention later, with the permission of the House, to spend about $9.5 million on these projects in 1973-74.
We have often referred to the ongoing problem in our society of employment for younger persons among us. Canada has one of the highest proportions of youth in its population and labour force of any industrial nation. The rate of growth of this age group will moderate in the last half of this decade, but over the next five years we must meet the challenge and integrate these young Canadians into our economy and society.
At present, all groups of youth experience rates of unemployment above the adult rate. Previous experience indicates that even as unemployment decreases, the unemployment rate among youth will remain unacceptably high, as it was throughout the 1960s. To meet this need we have taken or will be taking a number of steps. A youth employment division has been set up in the department, with youth consultants in each of our field regions. Manpower programs are being tilted to ensure access for these groups.
As an example of the situation we face, I would remind hon. members that young people under the age of 25 form 26 per cent of the labour force. They make up 40 per cent of our CMTP institutional trainees, 40 per cent of LIP workers and 63 per cent of training-on-the-job trainees. We shall be setting up various pilot projects to develop innovative solutions to the problems presented by youth unemployment. We are establishing special student CMCs for the summer months. Consideration is being given to the establishment of special youth units in our regular CMCs, staffed by younger workers. Mobile units will take our services to youth if they will not come to us. We are planning a co-operative approach with the provinces to improve career couselling data for youth and build better bridges between the worlds of school and work.
We have recently devised an experimental program in Toronto, called CRUNCH, to assist youth operated co-

operatives and businesses. We shall be evaluating this experiment very carefully to see where it might take us.

I will be pleased to elaborate on these activities at the first opportunity.
I am sure many hon. members know that I have a particular interest in the problems of our native people. I am anxious to ensure that they have equal access to Manpower programs and services and that their special needs are understood and met. LIP has been particularly beneficial to native groups. We have been impressed by the quality of the projects and the responsible manner in which they were carried out. I expect our new special programs for workers with particular employment problems will also be of particular benefit to natives. In the short time available to me I have been able to touch upon only a few aspects of our new approach. I look forward to a comprehensive examination and discussion of these matters when my department's estimates are before the committee. I appreciate the indulgence of the House in allowing me to continue past the time allotted to me. I have tried to condense my observations, in these circumstances. I look forward to the opportunity of dealing with these matters in more detail when my estimates are before the Standing Committee on Labour, Manpower and Immigration, at which time I hope to have the advice of members of the committee as to ways in which we can continue to improve our approach to job finding and job training, as well as other aspects of the work of my department.
