subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-GOVERNMENT FAILURE RESPECTING NEGLIGENCE OF UNEMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, despite the many plans to reduce unemployment outlined by the government in the various programs it has put forward, as well as in the budget, unemployment is still with us and rearing its ugly head as high as ever.
Many of us are aware that a small percentage have unlawfully milked the unemployment insurance fund. It is only right and just that they should be ferreted out and brought to task. However, in doing so many legitimate claims have either been delayed or stopped, causing severe hardship to families in dire need, especially at this time of year. The skyrocketing price of food has added to the misery of those in need.
I read recently the report of the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gillespie) who stated that one-third of the families in rural Canada live in poverty. He quoted Statistics Canada as stating that 32 per cent of families in rural areas in 1971, the last year for which statistics are available, had incomes below the so-called low income line. The figure for 1969 was 36 per cent. While the situation has improved slightly for families, for unattached individuals it is even worse. Of such individuals, 56.1 per cent were below the low income line of $2,013 in 1971, while 50.4 per cent were below the 1969 line of $1,894. It is up to us to try to find jobs for these people so they may regain their self-respect.
We hear about pockets of poverty and disparity throughout this great country. Some planners have suggested that the people to whom I have referred be uprooted and moved to urban areas to find work. These people do not want to leave their homes and friends to live in concrete jungles. Furthermore, this is no solution as it would aggravate the urban housing problem, where land is at a premium, and any new housing would be beyond their means. Surely a more sensible and cheaper plan would be to provide jobs in rural Canada.
The Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Jamieson) could come to the fore in this regard by giving us the suggestions which I understand will be forthcoming to provide new guidelines which I hope will bring in new areas of rural Canada which are no longer eligible. I can certainly speak with some authority on this matter because in my own region of Parry Sound-Muskoka the economic situation is very poor and we are no longer designated. Instead of hearing about the Minister of State for Urban Affairs, it is about time something was done to change this title or create a new minister of rural affairs. We always hear about the great cities. It is about time somebody spoke up for rural Canada.

March 12, 1973
Unemployment

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-GOVERNMENT FAILURE RESPECTING NEGLIGENCE OF UNEMPLOYMENT
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-GOVERNMENT FAILURE RESPECTING NEGLIGENCE OF UNEMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
It is in this area that the economy needs to be bolstered. There is no problem of land banks being needed in these areas to try to assemble land: there is all sorts of land. What they need are regular banks which will provide funds for jobs, housing, small industry, and so on. This is a must. This would keep our people in familiar surroundings where they are much happier. More jobs would be provided by our many businessmen as increases in sales and services warranted.
This morning I heard His Worship Mayor Drapeau on television giving a patriotic pitch for the great city of Montreal. He stated at the top of his voice, "We are number one". However, it was pointed out to him that number two was breathing hotly down his back and that the great city of Toronto would probably be passing Montreal before very long. The mayor said everything indicates that the people are leaving rural Canada and are heading to the big cities. The federal and provincial governments must take steps to stop the steady migration to our larger cities.
The many land controls are hurting small municipalities the most, much more than the larger cities. Little or no building is allowed, because it does not conform to the master plan. As a result, many small contractors and carpenters are sitting around doing nothing. Their employees are drawing unemployment insurance. All this is because they cannot get their lots approved. The situation would be much easier if these lots were approved. They are satisfactory in all respects; however, they are held up by government red tape, planners and civil servants some of whom are neither civil nor servants.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-GOVERNMENT FAILURE RESPECTING NEGLIGENCE OF UNEMPLOYMENT
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-GOVERNMENT FAILURE RESPECTING NEGLIGENCE OF UNEMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
This particular time of year, with what seems to be the spring breakup at hand, is the most serious for high unemployment in my constituency. I am quite sure the same situation prevails in a great many other rural constituencies. Lumbering in the bush is finished; tourist operators who cater to snowmobilers will not have any more visitors until the fishing season opens.
I checked with the Parry Sound office today. I was told that there are over 900 on the unemployment rolls. The total population of the area is quite small. There is a real problem there with girls-and I do not mean in the way some people might think. There is a problem of providing jobs for the female population. I am told that some did accept work outdoors, cutting and piling brush. They are to be commended for this; it shows the type of energetic people there are in my constituency. If the local Manpower authorities were given discretionary power to work out some plan with tourist operators and service industries whereby these girls could be paid part unemployment insurance benefits, and the employer part, they would be hired ahead of time to fix up tourist establishments, painting and for other things. Everyone would benefit. It could be said that we would be subsidizing an employer and he would be paying less than the minimum wage, but surely something could be done about this. The local Manpower office could have authority to investigate these cases and to ensure there were not any abuses.

I am aware that the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Andras) has a tough job. I listened to his remarks. He is to be commended for doing a pretty good job, but he has to sell more than himself. I remember seeing a movie many years ago; I think it was entitled "The Unholy Three". I suggest that the three who are holding up a great deal of the growth in rural Canada are the following: the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner), the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion and the Minister of State for Urban Affairs. If these three could be sold the idea of disgorging some of their untold millions to provide jobs and industry in rural Canada, it would greatly help the unemployment problem. It would also help the large cities, because they do not want more people looking for jobs.
I understand I have another two minutes, Mr. Speaker. I will let someone else use them. We all know the problem: we all see the headlines which state that the number one target is jobs. The real issue is jobs. The lists of jobless soar; that is the problem in a nutshell. We require more jobs, particularly in rural Canada.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-GOVERNMENT FAILURE RESPECTING NEGLIGENCE OF UNEMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would ask my colleagues not to applaud too long, because I am only allowed ten minutes.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to point out that there was earlier some kind of misunderstanding, I believe. I had been asked, as a special favour, not to take the floor before six o'clock, in order to enable the minister to make his speech, and I was supposed to speak after him. I suggest that you were not aware of this agreement, Mr. Speaker; at any rate, I am the second member to take the floor after the minister and I am satisfied with my lot.
I listened with great interest to the minister's statement about unemployment. I suggest that had he had more time, he might have talked about the other part of this motion which bears on the mismanagement of the Unemployment Insurance Commission. Nevertheless, the minister did say that unemployment is a disease that we must try to cure and, as a remedy, he suggested what the present government has always proposed, namely grants to industry, to local initiatives projects, to the Opportunities for Youth program, etc.
But this is not what will solve the problem of unemployment. Unemployment is not a disease by itself; it is only the result of over-production, of automation. Let us not forget it: unemployment is not a disease but a normal consequence. This problem must be solved through amendments to the act in order to enable the people to contribute to our country's wealth.
This is not a matter of full employment, Mr. Speaker. Full employment will never exist in the future. Today, just like before, we are told again and again: we must earn our living through our work. The minister, I suggest, still believes in it. Let us concern ourselves with the garanteed income, which will solve the unemployment problem, rather than with full employment. From what the minister said, you would think we are still in the 50's when work equalled production. Today, work is roughly 30 per cent manpower. It is that 70 per cent that needs to be redis-
March 12, 1973

tributed and it will not be redistributed by taxing those who have the chance to work in order to try and give a little money to the others and doing everything for the big interests which are presently running the country. We are giving all possible protection to big capital which is stockpiling the incomes of the country by the billions and we let the people drift by shouting at them: We are going to create employment. Let us stop this nonsense and start thinking not in terms of stop gap measures but in terms of long term remedies.
I suggested recently as a long term remedy to bring about massive relocations to allow society and individuals to reach consumption. I suggested for example to grant the old age security pension at 60. This way we could put 400,000 workers on retirement, and 400,000 unemployed could draw their living from industry.
That is what we call long-term reforms which would really remove the unemployment plague. In fact, I think that by taking such logical steps in order to ensure a minimum guaranteed income for everybody, we would apply an efficient measure.
I shall not dwell on this because I would like to deal with another subject. But when the hon. minister says that the number of jobs is increasing, he should add that it is because automation has been discarded. We have now stopped progressing because the more a country progresses, the more unemployment increases if we keep the same system. That is why it is absolutely ncessary to find other horizons and not be afraid to replace old methods by new ones. It has been done at the level of production. Why should we not do it at the level of redistribution? The state is such at a loss when it comes to redistributing, that one would think we were back in the starvation years. No, we are in a period of overproduction. Surpluses everywhere. Let us find means of redistributing this overproduction.
Mr. Speaker if I go on talking on unemployment and all the unemployment insurance offices, I shall not have time to say a word on unemployment insurance itself which should be my main subject this evening. I have been wanting to talk on this subject in the House for a long time, since the beginning of the session. Concerning the unemployment insurance about which everybody complains we wonder who is responsible. I say the main responsibility first lies with super-centralization both in Quebec and in all the other provinces. I think we have caught the virus of technology. We want to mechanize everything, we want to "electronize" everything in the shortest time period possible without thinking of the consequences. They have also succeeded in dehumanizing everything. It is the greatest social disaster of our age.
The first result of all that is the astronomical cost of administration, in which personnel is increasing constantly. I heard the minister saying just now that the largest increase in employment has been in administration, although the government tried to have us believe that automation would probably reduce it. This can also be attributed to ignorance on the part of promoters and of the machine operators or so-called technicians in these administrative centres. I believe that it is in computer centres such as the one in Montreal that the biggest mistakes are made. When I heard that they were going to
Unemployment
employ 133 new inspectors to seek out offences by the general population, I felt that they would have done better to send those 133 employees to work their infernal machines in Montreal, and look for the mistakes there.
That is where the real mistakes are, Mr. Speaker. Last winter, for instance, I have seen series of $500 and $600 cheques made in duplicate and sent in duplicate to the same unemployed worker. This was not done purposely by the recipient but by the Montreal centre which sent the cheques. When the worker was complaining too much the order was given to issue cheques and I have seen series of $500, $800, and $900 cheques issued in duplicate. And now we hear of overpayments. So as to cover up this affair, inspectors are dispatched to inquire from the unemployment workers and try to find out something.
We have reached the point where we no longer have time to do our job as members of Parliament. We have turned into employees of the Unemployment Insurance Commission. At home on weekends as early as ten o'clock on Saturday mornings I start working in unemployment insurance until midnight; on Sundays I start again as soon as I get up until six o'clock and then I board the 6:30 train to Ottawa.
In my opinion the current situation can be corrected. I think that the government has been had by the computer manufacturers and here is proof. I had question No. 1172 put on the order paper to know more about it. It is impossible to have further information elsewhere in connection with those computers. I have asked the following question:
1.	Were the computers installed in five Unemployment Insurance Commission head offices (Moncton, Belleville, Montreal, Vancouver, Winnipeg) purchased or rented?
This is what I would like to know. What deals were made in connection with those machines? And I further quote:
2.	(a) On what date were they purchased or rented (b) were they new or second-hand (c) at what price (d) if paid by instalments, under what terms and at what interest rate (e) how much was paid for maintenance from the date of purchase to December 31, 1972 (f) how many persons did these computers replace (g) how much was paid to American experts for the installation of these computers (h) how many people are assigned to maintenance?
Because we had not one single expert in Quebec able to operate those computers.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-GOVERNMENT FAILURE RESPECTING NEGLIGENCE OF UNEMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I congratulate you upon your election to office and the manner in which you and your deputies act as guides to those who are new to the customs and traditions of this House. It is indeed well to be led by men such as yourself in these ways.
I support strongly the statement made in this want of confidence motion. The government has not taken effective measures to provide more long-term jobs. This government has consistently refused to cut taxes sufficiently to stimulate the economy. It persists in taking millions of dollars, indeed hundreds of millions of dollars, from the private sector for its own use at a rate much higher than any industry would dare.

March 12, 1973
Unemployment
The short-term programs, at least in my riding of Niagara Falls, have been at best a mixed blessing and at worst failures. We had one Opportunities for Youth program that was carried over this past winter into a local initiatives program. What this program did-I spoke with the young people last Friday-was create a dependency among the senior citizens, a dependency which they did not feel before as deeply as they will when the program is phased out. The young people are discouraged and cynical, and the old people will be left with nothing.
For two years a patrol has existed on the Chippawa Creek. This program, too, is being phased out. It was an active life-saving venture. Tourists come from all over the world to visit Niagara Falls, but I am informed that this program will not be repeated. A local church commenced a local initiatives program last winter. The work was done and the church was completed but unfortunately, due to some administrative bungling, this group is involved in a big dispute with the LIP people. Certainly this is not very conducive to confidence in the government or the system.
During the election I had the opportunity to visit a factory in Fort Erie which at one time employed 3,000 men, yet for two years it has not been able to do very much because this administration cannot make up its mind about STOL aircraft. The men involved sought out an on the job training program but were informed that they could not carry it out in the proven way. This whole matter goes back to World War II, but this program must be worked into the inflexible patterns of the government and training is required before on-the-job training can be obtained. They cannot include such training through this program and bring employment to Fort Erie.
That is the pattern in the Niagara riding. It is a pattern of short-term job creation that does some good but also leaves tragedy in its wake for the old and the young. It seems that the patterns that have proved of use can no longer be followed. I am certain this pattern is duplicated in cities, towns and villages across the country.
There are 17,000 unemployed in the Niagara region, yet men speak to me on each side of the coin. They speak to me as unemployed and as employer. The unemployed and the employer alike never seem to indicate that they received a man through Manpower, or a job through Manpower, and many people have phoned and told me they had to phene Office Overload in order to get a job. Perhaps the free enterprise system could do somewhat better than this system appears to be doing.
It was rather interesting last week to note that one of the ministers made a foray into the last Liberal area of this peninsula, the whole of which was a Liberal stronghold before the last election. He said we were obstructionists and put forth no policies. We have put forth two practical policies. We have recommended massive tax cuts to stimulate production, not just to give a warm bath but to give great stimulus followed by the realization that you have to put this stimulation into productivity, not into inflation.
The Liberals ignored our other platforms, at least until the cold shock of October 30, and are now calling our policies billion dollar giveaways, or so their lord and master said last week. One of these days they will accept

these policies just as they have accepted the constant dollar theory and others we have presented in the past.
What is needed is a workable job-employee matching service and the return of local decision-making to the Unemployment Insurance Commission so the officials can sign cheques for the people, rather than having to send them away to the computers be they at Belleville, Montreal or wherever. There has to be some discretion in the hands of our experienced and very excellent civil servants such as those we have in the Niagara Falls area. Short-term solutions are no solutions at all. They just draw the people out of the work force and phase down the statistics. And even then, unemployment has not dropped to the level of 6 per cent for any length of time.
The people of the Niagara Falls riding need a bold frontal attack on unemployment through job creation in the private sector. Successive Liberal budgets have promised, but have failed to do this. Successive Liberal ministers have stated that all will be well, but the land is still not strong. I would suggest that until we have a more dynamic program, the people of the Niagara Peninsula, of Ontario and of Canada will suffer what this motion refers to-lack of initiative and lack of any programs on the part of this government.

speechtext:
I should like to tell my Creditiste friends that I hope they appreciate the fact that I put forward socialist points to their credit. Even though this is their motion, I hope they will allow me.

I was intrigued by the minister's statement, and that is another element which has thrown my notes into a jumble. I think his statement was indeed well meaning and, if anything, liberal with a capital "L" as well as a small "1". We were told by the minister that unemployment is a problem compounded of many factors-seasonal factors, regional factors, structural factors and factors which could be called generally social factors such as the matter of discrimination against certain types of people who are looking for employment. This is very very good, but not very new because we have been entertaining measures in this House for many years in this kind of categorization.
In the early 1960s we were able to look at the whole problem of unemployment and break it down into certain factors. Not only were we presented with these factors but
March 12, 1973

were presented also with traditional solutions. There was a certain amount of talk about the effects of fiscal and monetary policies needed to stimulate the economy, some reference back to the budget and some mention of policies which the minister himself admitted were in effect band-aid policies. There was even an admission that we had in our society what could be called and what was indeed called hard-core unemployment. It is very good that we recognize the existence of hard-core unemployment just as in our society we have come to recognize the existence of hard-core pornography. If we can face up to a fact perhaps we will do something about it. I presume we do not want to carry that analogy too far, but at any rate I believe hon. members get my point.
For a moment I should like to dwell on the matter of expansionary policies, not only because it is mentioned on the other side of the House but also because it is a frequent topic used by my colleagues in this corner. It is getting to be a fact that many modern economists, if very few modern politicians, now realize that the effect of expansionist policies is on the price level or the exchange rate rather than on the real things such as output, employment or unemployment.
What I am suggesting is that we may be all kidding ourselves that we are making the world better by tinkering with the model we have in our minds about the economy. Surely after the all these years of tinkering in this fashion and involving ourselves in expansionist and eoun-tractionist policies, consumptionist policies and overcon-sumptionist policies, we should know that we still have not attacked the basic problem. For the past dozen years or more we have had a fairly steady and rather obscene level of unemployment in this country. All the good intentions of the government which we have witnessed, and indeed the criticisms of government policy, have not done very much to reduce this level of unemployment.
Almost all public and private effort is designed to increase production and productivity. Let us admit that, whether the government side of the House says we shall take these measures to increase productivity and production, or whether this side of the House says, "All right, fellows; move over and we will do it even better than you can", we must face up to the very simple conclusion that if we increase production and productivity we will also increase unemployment. It is as sure as night follows the day that if we put better and more capitalization into industry, industry of course will use this capital to buy machinery, which has the purpose of increasing productivity which means, in other terms, the purpose of decreasing the number of jobs. So perhaps we should now, at this time in our history, start asking ourselves whether the very language we use in speaking about this problem is fitting and proper language.
For example, here is some heresy. Unemployment as such is not bad: what is bad is not having any money or not being paid. There are many people in our society who are unemployed or underemployed, but who are paid. I need not go through a list, but you can imagine the categories I have in mind as well as I can. They manage to live in effective human dignity while being unemployed or underemployed but relatively well paid. What we have to look at, really, is not simply the matter of job creation but
Unemployment
what we do with the leisure we are creating with all our new measures to increase capitalization and productivity. In other words if we can believe that our present unemployment is good for the rich, then it should also be very good for the poor.
One thing our advance is producing is the release of people from the necessity of working in the production of goods and services that we absolutely need in society. As people are being released from the need and the necessity to provide our standard of living and means of subsistence of course they are being displaced into another sector. Thank God that the system now provides for most of them and if their work is not needed in one sector they are taken up by another sector, the private sector in the main, and given jobs so that they can earn remuneration to buy the products of our society.
The problem with this kind of release and redirection of personnel is, first of all, that it is not very rational and, secondly, that it does not work toward increasing the quality of our lives. For example, if we reduce the number of people needed in basic production, they can go to the service industries and rather than working in essential and valuable areas we find them employed more and more in areas that, at best, do not enhance the quality of existence but increase the banality of existence. I can foresee many people being released from the drudgery of boring, productive activity working to build a society which is surfeited by an endless plethora of Kentucky-fried chicken stands.
Let us see if we can look at a few basic notions which might help us tackle this problem. First of all, let us try to spread the employment around. Why not have voluntary retirement at age 60? Why not have a sabbatical year for working people? As an academic, I always had the possibility in the future of having a sabbatical year. If it is good for me and for my colleagues, then it should be good for working people. Why should we not look at this way of spreading employment around? Why not begin to redefine what we mean by a regular job. Does a man have to work in the same factory 40 hours a week for 50 weeks of the year, or is there another way to approach what is meant by a regular job so that a young person, for example, could work less than that but work as part of a family unit, so that the young man and young woman could at least say they hold down regular jobs which give them the benefit of pensions, security, unemployment insurance, health premium payments, and so on? I would strongly suggest that such an approach would do much more to liberate women than the rather brief suggestions the minister made on that topic in his address.
If we spread employment around, we should think of spreading the pay around. It is strange that when talking about unemployment, employment and remuneration we hear nothing more these days about a good minimum wage. In my view, a good minimum wage is one which is so high that certain sectors of our economy scream. If it is not that high, it is not an effective minimum wage. I would like to talk about one point made by the author Paul Goodman. He said that the more a person's work is hard, the more a person's work is useful and necessary, the more a person's work is in the public realm, the less that person gets paid. Surely if this House really cares about

March 12, 1973
Unemployment
helping out the people who are the working poor, and the poor, they would do something significant about spreading the pay around and increasing the minimum wage standard.
We hear of all kinds of band-aid philosophies and floss programs, the sort of unemployment, worklessness and paylessness we have should make us realize that people want a job they can do, at pay which will allow them to live decently. It is no more complicated than that. That should be our basic objective.
When it comes to jobs that people can do, you will ask: How do we create the jobs? The need for jobs is there. There is all kinds of work that can be done in our society and all kinds of new services that can be effectively provided, but the fact is that the effective demand is not there. Since we are in the habit of borrowing ideas from the south, we can borrow one idea that has been emerging there in the past few years, that is, the notion of the state as employer of last resort.
Mr. Speaker, if you will not rise from your chair for thirty seconds, I will complete what I am saying. The state, at the federal, municipal and provincial levels could direct, through itself, people who want to be involved in work into all kinds of projects organized, not necessarily by the state itself but by the various voluntary associations in our society, such as the churches, and so on, and effectively hire people at this minimum wage. I will end by giving you one figure, Mr. Speaker.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on last Tuesday, March 6, the hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) introduced the following motion. I quote:
That this House expresses its lack of confidence that the combination of the corporate tax reductions and accelerated depreciation write-offs contained in the Budget of May, 1972 and proposals contained in the Budget of February, 1973 constitutes an adequate and equitable response to the needs of the country.
Today, we have the following motion proposed by the hon. member for Abitibi:
That this House deplores the continuous increase in unemployment, as well as the refusal or negligence of the Government to propose effective measures for providing more jobs of a remunerative character for Canadians, and condemns the existing authorities for imposing or tolerating quasirepressive measures affecting citizens who merely want to see respected their fundamental right to a decent standard of living and their personal dignity and to live in a climate of freedom and security.
Both motions are strangely similar and they are using up two debating days which are not producing much that is new or constructive on the part of the opposition parties.
I would like to refer to the budget speech of May 8, 1972 which said that the government's responsibility to Canadians was to protect already existing jobs, to look for means

to increase them and consider the situation in other countries of the world.
Then it was easy to see that a new protectionist instinct prevailed in the United States which was and is still trying to protect its trade and dollar; that the European Common Market-of which Great Britain has now become a member-was in full expansion and that some of our most traditional trade relations were in danger; that Japan had come back to life and that we, whose survival depends on international trade, were right in the middle of it all.
In fact, on each dollar that we put in our pockets or purses, 25 cents come from our exports. So our economy is vulnerable and Canadian prosperity depends on our capacity to compete against Europe, the United States and Japan, not only on foreign but also on domestic markets because of our imports. And to compete with other countries our businesses must be in a strong position vis-a-vis those other countries.
That is why, Mr. Speaker, the budget introduced in May last provided incentives to industry and manufacturing fighting against world competition in the form of a 40 per cent reduction in their tax rate. It was not intended as a gift or social aid but to allow Canadians to survive, compete and expand so they can have competitive prices, create jobs, sell on foreign markets and earn this quarter of each dollar which allows us to live and prosper.
As far as the various industrial incentives go, whether they are found in our tax system or in the form of regional incentives intended to give equal job opportunities across Canada, some have called them "corporate welfare" and their recipients "corporate welfare bums". In any case I do not like those expressions, whether they are applied to corporations or people.
Moreover, the basic goal pursued by the federal system through taxation of business concerns and a wide range of government policies and programs to stimulate Canadian industry is not social assistance to companies, but the welfare of the people. The main objective of all such measures is to help Canadian industry achieve some specific goals.
As I said earlier, the first objective is to meet increasingly keen competition from foreign companies in both domestic and foreign markets.
In the second place, we want to assist Canadian firms in modernising their facilities, increasing their productivity and bringing down their costs in order that they may compete more successfully with other countries. We want to enable them to manufacture new and improved products and to develop peak techniques, living as we do in an era of technology.
Finally we want to help Canadian firms to offer better job opportunities throughout Canada.
For instance, Mr. Speaker, those steps are basically meant to enable Canadian industries to increase their production and their investments with a view to creating, immediately, productive, permanent and remunerative jobs for our ever increasing labour force. In Canada, it is the private sector and not the governments which constitutes the real element of growth in production, jobs and true income.
March 12, 1973

Some claim that government measures and programs have been a complete disaster in terms of creating new jobs. I say to them that Canada is doubtless facing one of the toughest economic challenges in the world: the number of men and women, and more specifically of young men and young women, entering the labour market is growing much more rapidly than in any other country in the world.
Let me quote a few figures that clearly illustrate the challenge we face. From 1965 to 1970, that is a period of six years, our labour force grew by 1,440,000 new workers, in other words by 20 per cent. That increase of 1,440,000 workers over a six-year period exceeded by 100,000 workers the total increase, not on a percentage basis but in absolute terms, of the 15 most important industrialized countries in Europe. I am speaking of countries like England, France, Germany, Italy and Sweden.
In other words, our labour force comprised 100,000 more job seekers than the total number of newcomers on the labour market in 15 European countries, whose total population is 13 times and a half larger than ours. Such is the economical problem caused by the arrival of newcomers on the labour market.
And how many jobs have we created during that same period? From 1965 to 1970, we created 1,300,000 new jobs in Canada. We have offered 400,000 more jobs than the 15 European countries taken together whose population is 13 times and half larger than ours.
What a tremendous challenge it was and still is; and the present government and the whole country have succeeded in taking up the most important economical challenge ever faced by the world. In relative figures, employment has increased 57 times faster in Canada than in the United States, twice as fast than in Japan, seven times faster than in Germany and 27 times faster than in the 15 European countries I have mentioned.
Mr. Speaker, in order to guarantee their jobs to hundreds of thousands of Canadians throughout the country, the federal government must at all cost implement the measures advocated in the budget of last May. Many of them are essential if industry is to compete with foreign companies enjoying the generous support of their own government. This is specially true in the areas of the country where economic growth and affluence depend essentially on the development of natural resources or in the areas where the federal government must grant special aid to ensure the development of secondary industries.
Mr. Speaker, I believe that this new plan has been designed to create a better balance between the need to preserve an atmosphere conducive to economic growth and the need to establish a more equitable tax system for all Canadian taxpayers. In last May's budget, there were also other social measures that have been increased in the budget of February 19. I would like to go quickly through the important points of this budget which has been called a budget for the Canadian family. For all taxpayers, there has been a 5 per cent tax reduction with a minimum of at least $100 and a maximum of $500. The basic exemption has gone up from $1,500 to $1,600 for single people and
Unemployment
from $2,850 to $3,000 for married couples. So, Mr. Speaker, 750,000 Canadians will not have to pay federal income tax.
The basic old age security pension has been increased. From April 1, it will go from $82.88 to $100 a month and the guaranteed income supplement added to the basic pension will make a total of $170. The guaranteed income for old age couples will be $325. Our system of guaranteed income for old people is the best in the world.
Moreover, in last February's budget, it was proposed to increase veterans' allowances to at least $151 for single people and to $257 for married couples.
Also, Mr. Speaker, for the Canadian consumer in general, we have abolished the federal tax on children's clothing and shoes. We have also abolished the federal tax on consumer goods such as clocks, toilet articles, cosmetics; we also have abolished the federal tax on confectioneries, soft drinks and fruit drinks; we have reduced customs duties on meats, out-of-season fruits and vegetables; we have also reduced customs duties on consumer goods that are not made in Canada such as drug, china, furniture, etc. All this, Mr. Speaker, in order to give-

Mr. Speaker, I am glad that in moving such a motion our Social Credit friends are giving us the opportunity to make known to the government our position and reactions with regard to the high unemployment rate in this country. I am also glad to see that the Quebeckers are rising to condemn the nonchalance and carelessness of the present government.
Naturally, it is not from the ranks of the opposite side that has come the censure of the government policy. This is obvious. Mr. Speaker, it seems evident that for our friends on the other side Quebec will never be anything but a producer of Parliament members.
As soon as the Speech from the Throne was presented and even recently when the budget was debated, we expressed the most severe criticisms against the government because of its inability, which is almost built-in, to put back on its feet the economy of Canada as a whole and of Quebec in particular.
The "just society" they talked to us about, the "just society" they take care not to mention today, has produced an unemployment rate which can rightly be described as having only increased regional disparities in Canada during the last five years.
In Quebec, unemployment rate was 6.5 per cent in 1968, 6.9 per cent in 1969, 7.9 per cent in 1970, 8.2 per cent in 1971, 8.6 per cent in 1972 and, as our colleagues opposite would say-"To keep is strong"-the rate reached the shocking level of 10.2 per cent in January 1973.,,
Mr. Speaker, it is not because the Quebec ministers of State, among others, will get shortly a salary increase that will place them above their federal colleagues that one must believe that Quebec has solved its economic problems. Far from it! That example only shows the Liberal congenital helplessness when it comes to identifying genuine priorities.

March 12, 1973
Unemployment
What picture can we now draw of the province of Quebec? Its industrial production grows at a much slower rate than elsewhere; there is a 10.2 per cent rate of unemployment in Quebec; areas like the Lower St. Lawrence and the Gaspe peninsula are being deserted by their inhabitants because cost-shared development programs produced more red tape troubles than realistic solutions. Its agriculture is deteriorating-whether in the Eastern Townships, in the lake Saint-Jean area or elsewhere- because of the lack of a three-or five-year milk policy plan and because of the government's delay in solving the vital problem of feed grains in the East. Therefore, young farmers are deserting the farms and will sooner or later increase the number of unemployed people in cities.
In another field, industries such as the shoe industry, are running to seed in Quebec for the benefit of an ill-disciplined impor policy; youg people by the thousands are coming out every year of the CEGEPs and specialized schools only to find themselves face to face with the spectre of unemployment for the white collar workers; a small private business staggering with great difficulty in St. Hyacinthe or elsewhere and which sees large multinational corporations receive substantial grants without creating, in many cases, any new jobs.
That is the economic picture in Quebec. And brother governments-brothers in the election fund as well as in the arrogance that power gives them-are content with slogans like 100,000 jobs in April 1970 and 300,000 jobs in February 1973 without giving any concrete specific plan on which to base their forecasts.
The past speaks for the future and the people of Canada, in Quebec as elsewhere, have no more reason to believe in the favorable results of the recent budget then they had in those of previous budgets. We know it now, the new budget is even less expansionary than that of May 1972 considering the present political and economic context.
On the short run in 1973-because it is in 1973 that thousands of families in Quebec as well as elsewhere in this country are affected in their cost of living as well as their human dignity by unemployment-this government is satisfied, as we have seen, with a shy winter works program, some capital injected in programs which are really more of a plaster than a valuable plan of action.
It was indeed rather later before this government launched its winter works program, so late that provincial government and municipalities, particularly in Quebec, could no longer plan seriously any efficient program for 1972-73. No planning with this government. And instead of laughing at the winter works programs advocated by the Official Opposition this government should have used its energies to plan them a year ahead as we advocated during the last election campaign
Mr. Speaker, we have already committed ourselves to providing small Canadian businesses with direct incentives to promote their expansion, to increase progress opportunities and create more jobs. We have proposed to allow Canadian citizens to deduct from their income taxes half of any amount up to $5,000 which would be invested in small Canadian businesses. And in this manner, personal income tax could be brought down to $2,500 for the full life of the investment. This investment credit program would aim to encourage investments in small businesses and stimulate their expansion.
Small business, in Canada, is a vital sector of our economy, consuming more goods and services, paying more taxes and creating more jobs than any other sector. This pattern would be both an incentive and an inspiration for the youth of our country which is asking only for new opportunities, new careers. And we should take into consideration, Mr. Speaker, that half of those who are seeking work in Canada are young people under 25.
That was an example of concrete remedial action in the framework of our program, and a demonstration of the urgent necessity for replacement of the present government team.
Mr. Speaker, unless we are prepared to see an increase in the number of those who are discontented, disillusioned and anarchists, and to risk recurrences o&Jhe events of October 1970-I say so earnestly and vigorously-the time has come for decisions of the kind I have just outlined.
Mr. Speaker, the people of Canada, and those of Quebec particularly, are weary of being bandied from one level of government to another, from one election to the next, from one slogan to another.
With regard to current unemployment, especially in Quebec, it is true that, to borrow the words of the fabulist, all do not die, but-for the time being-all are stricken.
The whole country, Mr. Speaker, is looking forward to the advent of a humane government, that is aware of the ills of the day and that is capable of daring.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all I wish to congratulate my colleague from Abitibi (Mr. Laprise), mover of the motion, on his excellent speech. To my mind, his was most constructive criticism and he suggested sound solutions. Whatever one may think, on rereading his speech, one realizes that it is really chockfull of ideas, including new suggestions to solve the problem now under discussion.
I must say also that I endorse his suggestions. I urge the government to consider and implement them as soon as possible: time is running short. At this point, in conscience we all have the imperative duty to help resolutely to solve the economic problem which distresses us. The suffering experienced by a vast number of families makes it rank first amongst our priorities and endows it with a sacred character. One only has to live in an area where unemployment is high and incomes are very low to be convinced of it.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to deal with one specific issue in the little time available to me, that is the Local Initiatives Program as a means to curb unemployment by creating new jobs.
The former Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Mackasey) stated rightly, during the last Parliament, that the program was directly intended to create jobs and thus provide direct income to those who did not have enough.
As it happened, the government widely advertised the program, raising many hopes in every area by suggesting

March 12, 1973

that the new policy would create many jobs by implementing various community works which can only be launched with grants offered under the program. The people believed in the sincerity of the government. Then serious projects were submitted from all areas, but too many were rejected without a valid reason being given to warrant this refusal. We Social Credit party members very well know that this refusal is basically due to a lack of money, the fact that credits have run out. And when the minister sees his funds have run out, he suffers from anaemia and he must turn down projects. This is what happens in many cases under the Local Initiatives Program.
Thus, discontent, division, jealousy sprang up among people when noticing that such or such project was approved rather than another. Mr. Speaker, as an example I would like to quote a letter I received today from the good reverend of a parish struggling with misery and poverty. I am speaking of Sainte-Apolline in my riding, a parish of 1,000 to 1,200 souls, a great number of whom are on welfare. So, faithful to my mandate, I make it a point of duty to be his spokesman because he says in his letter to me, and I quote:
I have just received from the Department of Manpower and Immigration a reply concerning the project which the Fabrique de Ste-Apolline has proposed under the Local Initiatives Program.
This year as last year, the department's reply was no.
Last year, the reply was negative, as it is this year.
The municipality of Sainte-Apolline has obtained the same reply as the Church Council, and this also for the second consecutive year.
I am extremely sorry about that.
Recently, on a recent TV program Politique Atout, Mr. Mar-chand spoke of distributive justice. These are fancy words, but the facts are altogether different. Last year, in our area, the parishes of Saint-Marcel, Saint-Just and Berthier obtained funds allowing them to achieve their respective projects. This year, the same parishes again get their funds for their projects. This is probably the new distributive justice, that is always giving to the same people, to the friends ... ? Who knows?
The points of suspension are quite meaningful.
Still more surprising is the fact that the parish of Berthier obtained last year a second budget to complete its project whereas, previously, for us the reply had been that the program budget was exhausted. Do they think that we are crazy? They know that that we cannot voice our opinion and they take advantage of it.
When I received the department's reply, I received at the same time a poster from the Canadian Catholic Organization for Development and Peace (an organization devoted to the underprivileged countries). I am sending it to you. All that is written on it concerns our condition, except that we must get out of it by ourselves. We can rely on nobody else. We should like to develop our area also, but our government refuses to help us because we represent nor a political gain nor a future market. In fact, our position is worse than that of the underdeveloped countries. Unfortunately, we are Canadians.
As I said above, we have nobody to speak on our behalf. Unlike the underdeveloped countries we do not have organizations as Development and Peace to carry our message. We still have the hon. member for our riding. Will you care to give us a voice, to transmit our message to those hon. members of Parliament? You 25789-63
Unemployment
may even invite them to come and visit us. But who will? This is what is so sad about it: we are not recognized.
Thank you for reading this letter to the end.
Denis Lepage, cure of Ste. Apolline,
Montmagny.
Your message has been conveyed, Father. And I shall go on fighting to get something for your area, as for all areas in my constituency, in my province and in my country.
What were these people asking for? The renovation of a hall for community meetings, for young people's recreation, for older people to meet in order to know and understand one another better and spend as much time as possible working for their salvation and achieving material things with the resources of the community.
What was needed for the municipality's project? Help in developing these surroundings, which are most suitable for the tourist industry. So there were two very sound projects.
Mr. Speaker, this Protestant minister is right in what he says about the third world. I have spoken about it several times, not only in the House but whereever I have had the opportunity of meeting the population, so as to arouse the sense of responsibility of those who have power over this third world that we rub shoulders with every day without really noticing. It is a third world within our national boundaries.
I saw the Local Initiative Programme as an invitation to youth, to those still capable of achieving something with financial assistance from the State, and as an encouragement to return to work, that work ethic which is alas disappearing, but which is a formidable God-given tool for making into "retail" what He put "wholesale" on earth. Whatever the nature of our activities, whatever the field in which we work, work has always been and will always be a tool to enable us to achieve something, and that is what these people want.
I therefore call on the government to make considerable extra funds available to the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Andras), so that he and his officials may in turn approve more projects, and so that the selection of these projects will not be subject to political pressures. But some advice should be sought at the source of the projects, from the persons responsible within the organizations, the intermediate bodies and the municipal councils. They are the ones who are in a position to advise the selection committees and to tell the officials about the degree of priority to be given to the most urgent projects in the community and in short.. .

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-GOVERNMENT FAILURE RESPECTING NEGLIGENCE OF UNEMPLOYMENT
speechtext: This is exactly what is being done.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-GOVERNMENT FAILURE RESPECTING NEGLIGENCE OF UNEMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
I am told that it is exactly what is being done. Then, I would like to know who are the ones who do so. I have often asked with whom we were to deal, but it is always a matter of secrecy.
It happened once that a project was approved; I was quite pleased, because it was the continuation of a longterm program meant to clean up a certain area and to enable the population to carry on summer-time recrea-

March 12, 1973
Adjournment Debate
tional activities, because there was no lake in the area. Then, this project was approved by the officials, the contract was forwarded and later, by telephone, there was a request to return the contract quickly because there had been a mistake. One can therefore imagine how carefully the projects are selected!
I was pleased to see that this project had been approved. Why? Because it was logical, sensible and it enabled 87 people to work and earn a living, instead of wondering every morning about what they were going to do, with the continuing rise in the cost of living and their income remaining the same.
And, for sure, if there is anyone who knows how to encourage young people to work very hard and try to get over the difficult period which we are going through, I think I am the one, because I have always assumed my responsibilities in this field, and I shall continue to do so. But, please, let us make sure that small distant communities get from the government the same amount of attention as do the larger centres, for we find in those small communities human beings who want to live. They want not only to exist, but also to live truly in their country. That is why it is imperative that the necessary means be taken to reach them.
I would like, in closing my remarks to ask once again that substantial credits be granted immediately, before the unrest grows, in order that a greater number of people be employed doing something constructive.
Mr. Speaker, I am not the one who will tell those working on LIP projects to take all their time because those are government programs. I am always aware of my responsibilities and we should all together try to make the people understand that even if those are government-financed programs, each and every worker must try to give the best performance possible for that is the way we will generate a responsible spirit in the workers, develop our country and make possible the distribution of that enormous wealth to the whole population. Thus the ugly image of misery within wealth which we are experiencing, when there are fewer and fewer rich and more and more poor will at last disappear. Some people do not like hearing those words but it is our duty to say them. We have been elected by our constituents to represent them, attack the problems, find solutions and as far as I am concerned, that is what I will do as long as I live.
