subtopic: POST OFFICE-POSSIBLE RESTORATION OF SIX DAY A WEEK DELIVERY
POST OFFICE-POSSIBLE RESTORATION OF SIX DAY A WEEK DELIVERY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, six years have elapsed since the former postmaster general, Eric Kierans, began the destruction of the Post Office Department in the name of efficiency. In sheer selfdefence during the intervening period, more and more businessmen began using Her Majesty's mails less and less, and the Post Office has become the best friend of Canada's burgeoning private delivery businesses. As an example, in Toronto, where five years ago there were scarcely any private agencies engaged in this business, the metro Toronto phone book lists today no fewer than 85 firms which are prepared to guarantee same-day delivery within the city of both parcels and individual mailed pieces. I state this to demonstrate that the Post Office Department is in deep trouble. Now that we have a new Postmaster General (Mr. Ouellet), I hope he will take action to resolve some of the current difficulties. I have been asking a series of questions over the last few weeks since this parliament began. I have gained the impression that the Postmaster General feels that all is for the best in the best of all possible worlds. I look at the official communications bulletin of tne Post Office Department for January and read:
Ouellet's tour is a big success.
In French it is even more emphatic in that respect: it reads:

The minister's tour was a complete success.

I suppose that means "an absolute success."

subtopic: POST OFFICE-POSSIBLE RESTORATION OF SIX DAY A WEEK DELIVERY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: POST OFFICE-POSSIBLE RESTORATION OF SIX DAY A WEEK DELIVERY
speechtext:
That is nice work, patting yourselves on the back, because it comes from the minister's own publication. This dedication to efficiency has committed the Post Office Department to the process of mechanization. The intricate part of this is the postal code, which is so complex that the people of Canada are having difficulty understanding it. This is demonstrated by the propaganda efforts which the Post Office Department has established to help Canadians to interpret the postal code.
The Post Office Department spent $289,000 on a calendar, a commercial gimmick that is usually restricted to private enterprise. It is distributing a credit card holder. I suppose that is to help the bankrupt Canadians who are paying excess taxation. It will hold all the credit cards that are necessary to keep afloat because of the irresponsible fiscal policies of this government. It is spending $500,000 on general advertising which features slogans such as "Keep two pairs of plus fours". The idea is to have some kind of simple formula which makes it possible to understand the postal code.
I have some suggestions in this regard. For the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) we might have a code such as 02B 4T8. For Senator Forsey, I2C 4C4, and for the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gillespie), as he negotiates the auto pact, it might be B4U 2R1. I think the
March 12, 1973

Post Office advertising suggests that after having come to these formulas, they should award the booby prize to the most successful formula. I would say that the Post Office Department should award itself the booby prize.
Not only are there problems of mechanization but at the moment rural and small town postmasters are having difficulty in getting a new contract settled. I am sure all members agree the rural post offices are the backbone of the nation's postal system. Mr. Kierans started a system of phasing out rural post offices. His successor, Mr. Cote, cancelled this, realizing that it was destroying our postal system. Unless an immediate settlement is obtained for the 8,000 rural and small town postmasters who are looking for a better contract than the one they now have, we shall be in serious difficulty. At the moment they receive as low as $1,000 a year. On an hourly rate, it is as low as 46 cents an hour, which is well below the federal minimum of $1.90 an hour.
Early decisions are necessary in coming to the solution of these negotiations. We do not want long, protracted negotiations like those which caused such an impact on the morale of the postal employees in connection with the agreement which has just been reached. The Post Office Department is being sued for unfair treatment when it took over the mail transportation in larger centres from the private contractors. At the time we said this was a mistake. I think there are official reports in the Post Office Department that stated it was a mistake to substitute public enterprise for private enterprise in this field. Obviously, this is being demonstrated in the action of the former mail carriers who are now sueing the Post Office.
Morale is low. Public good will has been dissipated. I trust the Postmaster General will do something to rescue our badly demoralized postal service. I have one final word on this score. The deputy postmaster general, speaking to the Canadian Circulation Audit Bureau Incorporated last Friday, indicated that he now knows where the problem is. They have introduced a bugging device that traces mail through the system. This is what Mr. Mackay had to say:
We knew our service wasn't what it should be, but we were perhaps inclined to blame it on weather conditions and inability of airlines to fly from point to point, thereby delaying our mail.
What we found instead was that the weather was a very minimal factor .. . Failure within our own processing system made up by far the majority of our breakdowns.
I say to the Postmaster General, "Physician, heal thyself."

speakerposition: Postmaster General
subtopic: POST OFFICE-POSSIBLE RESTORATION OF SIX DAY A WEEK DELIVERY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in reply to the hon. member I would like to say first that I am quite disappointed that he did not use his time to make meaningful proposals. It is quite easy for him to enumerate series of problems but I wish he had put forward a few suggestions which I would have accepted with much sympathy and which I would have tried to implement.
I would tell the hon. member that for many years our mail problems have certainly increased. If they have increased it is because unfortunately over the last 15 or 20 years no attention was paid to the deep transformation of
Adjournment Debate
the country, namely the exodus of people from rural to urban areas. The fact that each day in Toronto and Montreal some 5 million pieces of mail have to be sorted out demonstrates how urgent it is to mechanize our operations. That is what we undertook to do, that is what we are doing and that is what we will do. The mechanization of our operations will enable us to provide a better postal service.
The postal code to which the hon. member made a brief reference is an essential step that a great number of other countries have taken, and instead of making fun of it, the hon. member should use it because it has been applied in his own province, Manitoba, for two years. I should be interested to know if the hon. member knows by heart his own postal code and if he uses it.
I should ask him to make a campaign in favour of the postal code because it is to the extent that people understand they must use it that we will be able to provide a better postal service.
The hon. member referred briefly to legal proceedings. I think he will understand that since this matter is now sub judice I cannot deal with it.
But finally, since he dealt with several points, I should like to remind him that we are negotiating with rural postmasters. We are fully aware of existing deficiencies but negotiations are proceeding well and I hope that we will arrive at a settlement in the near future.
What we have been able to achieve with 28,000 postal workers, who signed a collective agreement-this, as the hon. member knows, is the first time we have arrived at an agreement with postal workers without facing a nationwide strike-proves that it is possible to reach agreements not only with all our employees, but also with our postmasters.
Far from sharing the hon. member's views, I believe that things are going much better in the Post Office department than formerly and that the Canadian public is entitled to hope that very shortly our automation, our postal code and our new labour contract will bring about better service in Canada.

speakerposition: subtopic
subtopic: FISHERIES-REQUEST FOR FEDERAL ACTION TO PROTECT SALMON SPAWNING STREAMS
FISHERIES-REQUEST FOR FEDERAL ACTION TO PROTECT SALMON SPAWNING STREAMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on January 25 last, as will be found at page 638 of Hansard, I asked the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Davis) a question which appears under the heading "Request for Federal Action to Protect Salmon Spawning Streams". I felt this topic was worthy of further exploration with the minister so I put it down for discussion during this adjournment debate. My question was:
In view of the indicated interest in the preservation of salmon spawning streams on the part of the government of British Columbia as evidenced by the suspension of logging in at least one salmon stream, is he prepared to request the approval of parliament for a beefed-up appropriation in order to catch up with the longstanding backlog of neglected salmon spawning streams in the province of British Columbia?

March 12, 1973
Adjournment Debate
The minister replied:
Mr. Speaker, we certainly welcome the newfound interest of the government of British Columbia in salmon streams on the west coast. We have included more money in the budget to clear these streams.
Naturally, it is the question of the amount of money in the budget about which I am curious, and it is the one which we may have to explore further. In fact, the minister did provide a somewhat expanded answer in the remarks he made to the annual convention of the United Fishermen and Allied Workers' Union in Vancouver on February 5, as indicated in the notes of his speech which were circulated by his department. He said in part:
But there are thousands of streams, some small and some not so small, which flow directly into the sea. They can also be highly productive in so far as species like salmon and trout are concerned. Their rehabilitation could add as much as 50 per cent to our catch of these fish in recent years.
He went on to describe how in his second year as Minister of Fisheries he launched an attack on the problem of debris in small streams and suggested that his approach was twofold. He said:
One, we spent several hundred thousand dollars a year tidying up the streams themselves; two, we stepped up our efforts to persuade the B.C. forest service that a total, environmental approach to river basins would pay off.
Later in his remarks he added to his view about the recent action of the government of British Columbia when he said:
__I was glad to see the action which B.C.'s lands and forests
minister, Bob Williams, took the other day. He backed our Fisheries people up on the Indian River.
That river is in my constituency, I may say. The minister went on to say:
This is a welcome change from the back-of-the-hand treatment we got from Ray Williston and some of his senior staff.
Should any member of this House think the minister's remarks were a little strong in that connection, I think any hon. member who recalls the situation that developed over the driving of logs on the Stellako River a few years ago, when the government of British Columbia insisted, in spite of a report signed jointly by officers of the federal fisheries department and the recreation and conservation branch of the provincial government that some 10 per cent of spawning in that stream was being destroyed by each year's drive, will know that I join the minister in welcoming some change in attitude. That fact is self-evident.
What about the question of providing more money? I have taken a quick look at the estimates for the forthcoming year. At this point I shall refer only to the description of the estimates of manpower and the increase in requirements. It is suggested there is an 8 per cent increase in the Manpower estimates for the fisheries and marine program, but the footnote says:
The increase is due primarily to the provision of increased protection services on rivers closed to salmon fishing, hiring of summer students and studies related to the Mackenzie Valley pipeline.
I take it the reference to increased protection refers to Atlantic salmon rivers. I suggest to the minister that he has a long way to go and that some of us will want to

explore this question very seriously with him when we get to the estimates. As I read them, there is certainly nothing which indicates any real beefed-up program, at least as far as the coming fiscal year is concerned. I say frankly to the minister and the government, in almost 20 years since I first came to this House, I have not known the morale of the field officers in his department to be so low and despairing as it is at the present time.
They say that walls have ears. Members of Parliament have ears, and certainly to my knowledge this is my assessment of the case. I have some pictures here which I shall be pleased to show to the minister in the committee. One is a picture of the Indian River taken one half mile from the beach. It shows a log jam which has been there for the last four years, and the results after four years of attempts by his department to do something about clearing that jam.
I suggest that unless there is a realistic approach to clearing these streams with proper equipment and a proper approach to the necessary manpower, our hope of increasing by 50 per cent the catch from the streams, to which the minister referred in his speech in Vancouver, is a long way into the future. So far as I am concerned, I intend to do everything in my power to see that the fullest co-operation is provided to the federal Department of Fisheries and the field service officers by the appropriate people within the government of British Columbia.
I hope the fact that the present minister of lands and forests is also minister of recreation and conservation is a real indication that the government of British Columbia is taking a serious look at this question in the hope that there is a genuine and complete ecological approach to our land use in respect of the rivers and streams of the province of British Columbia.

speakerposition: Minister of the Environment
subtopic: FISHERIES-REQUEST FOR FEDERAL ACTION TO PROTECT SALMON SPAWNING STREAMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Barnett), who is normally knowledgeable in fishery matters, knows that one thing he said tonight is wrong. He said that the morale of our fisheries officers on the west coast had never been so low. It's wrong for the following reasons. Never before have the fisheries officers on the west coast had as much leverage, so much influence over the practices of the logging companies and the foresters as they have today.
One of the reasons is the increasing co-operation they are receiving from the provincial authorities. The new government in British Columbia has put together two former departments. One dealt with forestry, in other words the handling out of forest management licences; the other dealt with fish and game and recreation. The two are now one in one department of the environment, although it is not yet called that.
It is now possible for the fisheries service on the west coast to deal with a single department so that they are able to reconcile the often conflicting claims of the wildlife and recreational people, on the one side, including fisheries, and forest management practices on the other.
There has been an increasing understanding of the problem on the part of the forest industry and the companies themselves. The foresters today are much more conscious of the fisheries resource, wildlife and the need to preserve the watershed for all purposes than they were
March 12, 1973

before. We have had very good co-operation from the industry. There have been many cases, of course, of logging practices which have continued to destroy salmon streams. For this reason we have to continue to prosecute companies. There have been several dozen prosecutions in recent years. The increase in this kind of discipline has helped the morale of our forestry officers as well.
The hon. member for Comox-Alberni asked about our budget on the west coast. The notes I have received from the department say that the budget and the Manpower commitment have been increased so as to improve our initiative in protecting salmon streams from bad logging practices. The professional staff located on the west coast, and incidentally assigned to deal exclusively with fisheries problems on logging streams, has been increased. An additional fishery officer has now been hired and he will concentrate solely on logging problems on the west coast of Vancouver Island which was an area about which the hon. member expressed concern.
The hon. member referred to an incident earlier this year involving the Staghorn and Indian Creek area of Vancouver Island. The departmental people arranged a meeting on January 3 bringing together the B.C. Forest Products Company officials, the B.C. forest service and a group of concerned private citizens. They discussed the problem of debris in the streams and the company agreed to cease certain logging practices and to set certain sections aside to remain in the natural state along tributaries of the streams where salmon spawn. After the B.C. forest service reported back, the minister of lands, forest and waters for British Columbia announced that it would require the company to do what it had agreed to do voluntarily at the meetings convened earlier by the fisheries service.
To sum up, the reasons why morale is high on the west coast have been enumerated. There is more co-operation from the provincial forest service, there is a great deal more co-operation with the logging companies, and with more prosecutions they are making considerably more headway than ever was the case in the past.

speakerposition: subtopic
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-REQUEST FOR WITHDRAWAL OF INVITATION TO PRESIDENT AMIN OF UGANDA TO VISIT CANADA
EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-REQUEST FOR WITHDRAWAL OF INVITATION TO PRESIDENT AMIN OF UGANDA TO VISIT CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on February 13 I asked the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) if he would consider this government's formal invitation to President Amin of Uganda to visit Canada in August of this year. To support my objections I cited the inhuman and inhumane policies of dictator Amin toward non-black persons in his country.
Needless to say, I was rather surprised when the right hon. gentleman answered that it was this government's view that it should not intervene in the affairs of other Commonwealth nations. Further, the Prime Minister said that there is no provision for expelling a member of the Commonwealth. I must reject the statement that this government has not intervened in the affairs of other Commonwealth nations. The record of this government's con-
Adjoumment Debate
demnation of Rhodesia, to name only one example, is all too clear.
As to the question of expelling Uganda from the Commonwealth, I did not say nor did I imply that we should seek the expulsion of Uganda from the Commonwealth. But since the Prime Minister has raised the question I will address myself to it in a moment.
I will deal first with my reasons for objecting to the Canadian government extending a formal invitation or any other type of invitation to such a person as General Amin. General Amin's psychopathic reign of terror since he became dictator of Uganda is well known to all of us here but I would like to refresh the memory of hon. members on a few specifics. All hon. members are aware of the expulsion from Uganda of some 40,000 Asians. Their only crime was their racial origin; and they were not only expelled, they were stripped of all their personal possessions. They were given 90 days to leave the country, and some of them were second and third generation Ugandan citizens.
Canada accepted a large number of the Asians, and it is to our credit that we did so. But I waited in vain for Canada to register its indignation and condemnation of the Uganda president's actions in the United Nations, or at least to the Commonwealth. Our silence throughout this degrading and inhuman experience indicates a certain degree of approval.
Reports from Uganda a few months ago described a most disturbing and revolting situation involving the Uganda dictator. It was reported that he ordered 20 or more prisoners who had been convicted of minor offences removed from a village jail and tied to tables in the village square. General Amin then moved among the tables and assisted a group of soldiers to beat the prisoners to death with clubs. The general said that this would teach the villagers respect for the law. In the same vein, highly respected reporters for Reuters, AP and other agencies say that Uganda's soldiers are empowered to go about the country selecting people at random to be tried by military courts for minor offences, or even on trumped up charges, and then shot to death in the village squares.
General Amin announced early this month that he would expel Kenyans living in Uganda and confiscate their property if Kenyan newspapers did not stop reporting on his policies and practices. He has served notice on other non-black people in Uganda that they are more or less living on borrowed time. Everything that President Amin does, everything he believes in runs counter to everything that we in Canada hold in reverence. We have laws to ensure that people are not discriminated against in any way because of their race, colour, religion or for any reason whatever. General Amin's personal conduct, his political policies and his official practices generate deep revulsion in the hearts of most Canadians, and I have never heard anyone suggest that this man is a civilized human being.
This brings me to the second part of the Prime Minister's answer, the fact that he would not direct the Commonwealth in any way that would involve the censure of one government by another. I cannot accept this. As I mentioned before, I cannot help but feel that many people today interpret our silence in this matter to indicate at

March 12, 1973
Adjournment Debate
least some measure of acceptance. In my view it is irresponsible of us not to register our condemnation of this revolting conduct on the part of a Commonwealth nation.
The Prime Minister said that there was no provision for the removal of a member from the Commonwealth, and while I did not suggest that it should be done I must say in retrospect that it is too bad that there is no provision to expel a nation from the Commonwealth. A nation such as Uganda and a dictator such as General Amin are out of step with the Commonwealth's aims and objectives. There is no way that he can contribute to the well-being of other citizens of Commonwealth countries. There is no way that he can contribute anything worthwhile to the Commonwealth as an organization. General Amin is detracting from the ideals and the objectives of the Commonwealth in everything he says and does, but as a member of our organization he is getting a free ride at the expense of the other members.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I would urge the Prime Minister to advise the President of Uganda that our government's invitation was in no way a formal or official invitation to our country. I would go so far as to suggest that the general would not be welcome at the Commonwealth conference in Canada in August. Failing that positive approach, I would at least ensure that the general was not accorded an official welcome when he arrives here. For our government to extend an invitation to General Amin to visit Canada implies a double standard in the conduct of our external affairs that I find objectionable and unacceptable and I urge the Prime Minister to reconsider his position in this matter.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-REQUEST FOR WITHDRAWAL OF INVITATION TO PRESIDENT AMIN OF UGANDA TO VISIT CANADA
speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker, but I wish to say that I understand quite well the reaction of the hon. member for Sherbrooke.
At all events, I shall continue the reading, in English, of the answer that was prepared for me.

This invitation represented our government's firm commitment to the Commonwealth and to the ideals which it espouses. As an association of nations which are at every stage of economic development, of diverse wages, cultures and institutions, the Commonwealth has the unique capacity to foster informal and intimate consultations concerning matters of common interest to the leaders of its 31 members.
As such, it is capable of exerting a beneficial influence in the promotion of international understanding and world peace. Nevertheless, one must remember that it is a voluntary association of independent sovereign states which derives its strength to promote international peace and progress from fruitful consultation and co-operation among its members.
The Commonwealth declaration issued by the heads of government at Singapore in January, 1971, affirms the association's belief in the benefits of fostering understanding among nations and firmly rejects coercion as an instrument of policy. Accordingly, the Commonwealth does not seek to impose policy upon its member states, particularly in the realm of domestic affairs.
Among the principles set out in the Commonwealth declaration is the statement that members-
-recognize racial prejudice as a dangerous sickness threatening the healthy development of the human race and racial discrimination as an unmitigated evil of society. Each of us will vigorously combat this evil within our own nation.
Membership in the Commonwealth, though stemming from a common heritage and tradition, is no less determined by a subscription to principles contained in the declaration. Yet there are no provisions for expelling a Commonwealth member for actions one or more nations believe to be contrary to the ideals of the association. The Commonwealth nations, however, can collectively express their displeasure if they so desire.
Canada's reaction to the expulsion of non-citizen Asian residents of Uganda is well known. Based upon the belief of all Canadians in equality and justice and the national inability to ignore the plight of human beings in need, we welcomed several thousand Ugandan refugees to Canada. This action was warmly welcomed by many within the

March 12, 1973

international community but especially so within the Commonwealth.
With regard to the forthcoming Ottawa meeting, it must nevertheless be borne in mind that each head of government of all the member countries is entitled to attend such meetings wherever they are held. The decision to hold a meeting is taken jointly by all heads of government, and it is always the hope and expectation that they will personally attend whatever potentially divisive problems there may be. The conference should not be expected to resolve such problems, but it would be a retrogressive step if they were allowed to prevent the meeting together of all heads of government for their traditional intimate exchange of views and their examination of the progress of a number of practical initiatives since the last meeting. Canada is now taking its turn as host to one of these meetings. Although this government strongly disagrees with the policy of expulsion undertaken by President Amin-
Adjournment Debate

Perhaps the Chair itself has a complaint to make to those who write such texts. Perhaps they should make them shorter, so that we can stick to the three minutes allocated for reply. We try to limit this period to 30 minutes, so that hon. members have seven minutes to express their views on the question they raised in the previous days and I think we must also ask the government spokesmen, whether parliamentary secretaries or ministers, to try and reply as much as possible within the prescribed time.
I think at this stage, it would be difficult to allow the parliamentary secretary, who has already exceeded by two minutes the time that was allocated to him, to complete his answer. Perhaps he could take advantage of the rest of the night to give it directly to the hon. member who raised the matter.
